purpose: The Perimeter — Kristy’s sourced answers for the parts of the store that have no barcode: produce, the butcher and fish counters, dairy, bulk bins, and the label terms used there. Entries are TOPICS, not flags: the perimeter answers questions, it does not score products. It is loaded separately from the ingredient KB and is NEVER fed into the verdict engine.

evidence_tiers.established: Strong scientific consensus, major health organization classification, or regulatory action in multiple countries. Settled enough to act on without debate.
evidence_tiers.credible_concern: Meaningful peer-reviewed evidence of harm exists. Debate is ongoing, but the signal is real and worth flagging, especially where a clean swap exists.
evidence_tiers.kristys_standard: The whole-food standard leads here even where regulators have not acted. Flagged as a standard, not as settled science. The difference is always stated.
evidence_tiers.time_tested: Foods with deep roots in human diets, eaten and trusted across generations, often long before modern studies existed. History is the evidence, and it is labeled that way. Absence of a clinical trial is not absence of value, and tradition is never dressed up as settled science.

no_answer: No solid answer on that one yet. Better said than guessed. The fish counter, the butcher, produce, dairy, the bulk aisle, and what a label term actually means are all covered.

entries.title: Wild vs. farmed salmon
entries.question: Is wild or farmed salmon better?
entries.decision: Wild salmon is worth choosing; farmed eats a plant-oil ration.
entries.why: Feed decides the fat, and a penned fish eats what it is given. Wild is the whole-food standard.
entries.short_answer: Two different animals sold under one name. Wild salmon eats krill and small fish across open ocean. Farmed salmon eats a formulated ration built largely on plant protein and vegetable oil.
entries.detail: That ration leaves farmed salmon with far more omega-6 and a much worse omega-3 to omega-6 ratio. Astaxanthin goes into the ration because the flesh comes out gray without it. Sea lice and the treatments used against them are the cost of penning fish that close together, and antibiotic use varies enormously by country of origin. The ratio is the claim, not the amount. Farmed salmon is fatter, so a serving can carry as much total omega-3 as wild or more; what the feed changes is the balance against omega-6, and that is the difference worth naming. Country of origin does most of the work on the rest: Norwegian farming runs close to zero antibiotic use on the back of vaccination, and other producing countries run far higher. The fish never swam anywhere, and it was colored to look like one that did.
sources: Alaska Sea Grant, University of Alaska Fairbanks “Aquaculture” https://alaskaseagrant.org/our-work/aquaculture/ (Alaska law limits aquatic farming to shellfish and seaweeds; salmon ranching by nonprofit hatcheries supplements, not replaces, wild stocks)
entries.kristy_take: Wild, and frozen wild before fresh farmed. Where wild is not in the case, the tin is.
entries.instead: Canned wild salmon, or sardines. Actually wild, and canned is the cheapest way to buy wild.
buying_tips: Frozen wild Alaskan is often cheaper and fresher than ‘fresh’ farmed that has been in transit.
Sockeye and coho are almost always wild, and their color is deep because of diet, not dye.
‘Fresh’ at the counter is frequently previously-frozen. Ask. It is not a downgrade.
watch_out: Atlantic salmon is farmed, effectively without exception. Wild Atlantic is off the market.
Frozen wild runs cheaper than fresh farmed, and it is the same fish, frozen at its best.
Antibiotic use on farms varies enormously by country of origin, so read the country before judging the fish.
Alaska law limits aquatic farming to shellfish and seaweeds, so Alaska salmon is not net-pen farmed. Hatchery ‘ranching’ there releases juveniles to supplement wild runs, not replace them.

labels_decoded.meaning: Required on the case label. On salmon it almost always means Atlantic in a pen.
Caught in the wild; Alaskan fisheries are well managed.

entries.tier_note: Frozen wild being the same fish is documented; reaching past the fresh Atlantic for it is the whole-food standard.
asked_as: wild or farmed salmon
is farmed salmon bad
which salmon should i buy

entries.title: Imported vs. domestic shrimp
entries.question: Is imported or domestic shrimp better?
entries.decision: Wild American shrimp is worth finding; most imports are pond-farmed.
entries.why: Country of origin is printed by law. It is the one sourcing question with an answer.
entries.short_answer: Most shrimp in US stores is imported and farmed, and what stands behind it varies enormously by country of origin. Wild American shrimp from the Gulf and South Atlantic is the one you can trace to a managed fishery.
entries.detail: Country-of-origin labeling is required on unprocessed seafood, which makes shrimp one of the few things in the store where the sourcing question has a printed answer. Farming practice, pond management and antibiotic use vary by producing country rather than by the word ‘farmed’, so origin plus a certification does more work than any claim on the front of the bag. Frozen raw shrimp gives the most control over how it is cooked, and usually the best value. Where the bag is farmed, a credible certification is what stands in for knowing the farm.
sources: North Carolina Sea Grant, Coastwatch “Curbing the Import Appetite: Selling American Shrimp in the U.S. Market” https://ncseagrant.ncsu.edu/coastwatch/curbing-the-import-appetite-selling-american-shrimp-in-the-u-s-market/ (pond-raised imports vs. wild-caught: flavor, size uniformity, appearance)
entries.kristy_take: Read the country first. It is printed by law and it is most of the answer.
buying_tips: Country-of-origin is required on the label. Read it before anything on the front.
‘Wild American’ or ‘Gulf’ is the traceable one.
Frozen raw gives the most control over the cooking, and usually the best value.

labels_decoded.meaning: Country-of-origin labeling — required, and worth checking.
Pond or tank raised; quality depends entirely on the operation.

entries.tier_note: Farm practices genuinely vary by origin, the concern is documented, and a certified bag is the clean swap.
watch_out: Where wild American is not stocked, check for a BAP or ASC certification. It stands in for knowing the farm.
‘Fresh’ at the shrimp case is nearly always thawed. Buying it frozen is the same shrimp, earlier.
Uniform size and a flawless look point to pond-raised. Wild shrimp come in a wide range of sizes and are graded to a count per pound.
asked_as: is imported shrimp ok
what shrimp should i buy
is farmed shrimp bad

entries.title: ‘Fresh’ vs. previously-frozen fish
entries.question: Is fresh fish better than frozen?
entries.decision: Fish frozen at sea is often fresher than what sits on ice.
entries.why: Most ‘fresh’ at the counter was frozen first. Flash-frozen at sea beats days in transit.
entries.short_answer: Not necessarily. Most fish at the counter labeled ‘fresh’ has been previously frozen and thawed. Fish flash-frozen at sea can be fresher than ‘fresh’ fish that’s spent days in transit. Frozen is often the smarter, cheaper buy.
entries.detail: Freezing at sea locks in quality within hours of the catch. ‘Fresh’ fish on ice may be several days from the water. Neither is a downgrade. But don’t pay a premium for ‘fresh’ assuming it’s better, and don’t re-freeze fish that was sold thawed.
sources: Alaska Longline Fishermen’s Association “Why Frozen?” https://www.alfafish.org/why-frozen (frozen rapidly to at least -10° F in a few hours of catch, often fresher than ‘fresh’ fish after days in transit)

Whidbey Seafoods “Why Flash-Frozen Seafood Is the Freshest Choice You Can Make” https://whidbeyseafoods.com/blogs/education/why-flash-frozen-seafood-is-the-freshest-choice-you-can-make (frozen almost immediately after being caught, often right on the boat; rapid freezing locks in freshness, flavor and nutrients, and no large ice crystals form, so texture and integrity remain)
entries.kristy_take: Frozen wild, without hesitation. Thaw it in the fridge overnight and nobody could tell.
buying_tips: Ask the counter ‘was this previously frozen?’ The answer is often yes.
Buy frozen and thaw at home for the best price and control.
Don’t re-freeze fish that was sold thawed.

labels_decoded.meaning: Frozen then thawed for display — common and fine; just don’t re-freeze.
Never frozen — but possibly several days old depending on transit.

entries.tier_note: How much of the fresh case was frozen first is a matter of record, not a suspicion.
watch_out: ‘Fresh’ on the sign says nothing about when the fish was caught. Fish frozen at sea within hours can be fresher than fish that spent days in transit to the counter.
Flash-freezing halts the degradation that takes texture and flavor. A fillet sold thawed has already used that advantage, so cook it rather than refreezing it.

is frozen fish worse than fresh
was this fish previously frozen

entries.title: Grass-fed vs. grain-fed beef
entries.question: Is grass-fed beef worth it?
entries.decision: Grass-finished beef ate grass its whole life; grass-fed alone did not.
entries.why: ‘Grass-fed’ allows a grain finish at the end. ‘Grass-finished’ is the whole-food standard.
entries.short_answer: ‘Grass-fed’ is a floor, not a standard. Cattle can graze most of their lives, eat feedlot grain for the last months, and still be labeled grass-fed. ‘Grass-finished’ or ‘100% grass-fed’ covers the whole life. That one is worth paying for.
entries.detail: The USDA withdrew its own grass-fed marketing standard, the AMS Grass (Forage) Fed claim standard, in 2016, so the bare claim now rests on the producer and on whatever third-party seal sits behind it. American Grassfed Association certification and Certified Grassfed by AGW both audit the whole life. The compositional difference that follows a grass finish is established and modest, and it is a leaner animal with a different fatty-acid balance rather than a different food. The fat profile follows the finish, not the start.
sources: peer-reviewed reviews of grass- vs grain-fed fatty acids
Federal Register 2016-00440 “United States Standards for Livestock and Meat Marketing Claims, Withdrawal” (govinfo.gov) https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2016-01-12/html/2016-00440.htm
entries.kristy_take: Both words, or it is a feedlot animal wearing a nicer sticker.
entries.instead: Grass-finished ground beef or chuck. The same standard, in the cut that costs the least.
buying_tips: ‘100% grass-fed’ and ‘grass-finished’ mean the same thing. Either one is the claim.
Ground and chuck are the cheapest way into a whole-life grass animal.
At the counter, ask what the animal was finished on and for how long.
watch_out: Where grass-finished is not on the shelf, organic grain-finished is the floor. Well-raised grain-finished beef beats poorly-raised anything.
Pasture artwork on the package is not a claim. The words are the claim.
A grass finish leaves a leaner animal, so it cooks faster and dries out at feedlot-beef heat.
USDA withdrew its grass-fed claim standard in 2016. A ‘grass-fed’ label today points at a standard the company chose, so ask whose definition it is.

labels_decoded.meaning: Ate grass at some point. May still have been grain-finished before slaughter.
Finished on grain in a feedlot. The US default.

entries.tier_note: What each of the two words is allowed to mean is documented fact. Insisting on the whole-life claim is a standard, not a finding.
asked_as: is grass fed beef worth it
grass fed or regular beef
is grass fed actually better

entries.title: Ground beef with liver and heart blended in
entries.question: Is organ blend ground beef worth it?
entries.decision: Organs named with their percentages: buy. ‘Organ blend’ with no numbers: pass.
entries.why: Regulation keeps organs out of ‘ground beef’, so a blend needs its own name and a full ingredient list.
entries.short_answer: Under federal rules, ‘ground beef’ is chopped beef only, cheek meat aside. A blend with liver or heart needs its own name and full ingredient list. The test is whether the label gives liver and heart each a share.
entries.detail: 9 CFR 319.15(a) defines ‘Ground Beef’ as chopped fresh or frozen beef, fat capped at 30 percent, no added water, binders or extenders, with trimmed cheek meat the one allowed addition and capped at 25 percent. A product with liver or heart in it falls outside that definition, and 9 CFR 317.2 then requires a common or usual name or a truthful descriptive designation plus a full ingredient statement in descending order. ‘Ancestral blend’ and ‘primal blend’ are producer names for exactly this product, not standardized terms. Two label examples: Force of Nature’s Ancestral Blend states 8 percent organ meats (4 percent liver, 4 percent heart, 92 percent muscle); Seven Sons’ Primal Blend states 92 percent ground beef, 5 percent liver, 3 percent heart. Liver is the retinol-dense ingredient: the NIH fact sheet lists pan-fried beef liver at 6,582 mcg RAE per 3 ounces, against a tolerable upper intake of 3,000 mcg a day for adults. The liver percentage on the label is therefore the number that matters. A blend that states its shares is plain ground beef with a measured amount of organ folded in. A blend that hides behind ‘organ blend’ or ‘ancestral’ alone leaves the liver share unknown.
sources: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, Vitamin A and Carotenoids, Fact Sheet for Health Professionals https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/VitaminA-HealthProfessional/
Force of Nature, Grass Fed Beef Ancestral Blend, product page (8% organ meats; 4% heart, 4% liver, 92% muscle meat) https://forceofnature.com/products/regenerative-beef-ancestral-blend
Seven Sons Farms, Ground Beef Primal Blend, product page (92% ground beef, 5% liver, 3% heart) https://sevensons.net/store/product/ground-beef-ancestral-blend
entries.kristy_take: A blend that prints its numbers is honest ground beef. One that will not is a mystery bag.
entries.instead: Plain ground beef and a small piece of liver from the counter. The share is whatever goes in the pan.
entries.cart_pick: Liver and heart beef blend, shares stated
buying_tips: Look for liver and heart named in the ingredient list, each with a percentage.
The product name will not say ‘ground beef’ alone; a blend has to carry its own descriptive name.
Grass-finished applies to the blend the same way it applies to plain ground beef. Both words, or it is a grain finish.
watch_out: Liver sets the vitamin A. By NIH figures, 3 ounces of pan-fried beef liver holds more than twice the adult daily upper intake. Check the liver percent and keep servings ordinary.

Two shares producers print are 8 percent organ, or 5 percent liver plus 3 percent heart. At those shares, both label examples say the blend tastes like regular ground beef. A pack with no shares gives no such reading.
‘Organ blend’ or ‘ancestral’ on the front with no shares anywhere on the pack is a pass, not a bargain.

labels_decoded.meaning: By regulation, chopped beef only. Trimmed cheek meat up to 25 percent is the one allowed addition; liver and heart are not.
A producer’s name for ground beef with liver and heart folded in. Not a standardized term; the ingredient list carries the shares.

entries.tier_note: The name rule is on record. Reading the ingredient list for each percentage is the ask.
asked_as: is organ blend ground beef worth it
what is ancestral blend beef
does the liver taste come through in blended ground beef
should i buy ground beef with liver in it

entries.title: Rotisserie chicken from the hot case
aliases: what is in a rotisserie chicken
is the deli rotisserie chicken injected
entries.question: Is the rotisserie chicken worth buying?
entries.decision: Chicken and salt on the label: buy. Phosphate and starch: pass.
entries.why: Every ingredient must be listed in descending order; a solution names its percent and contents.
entries.short_answer: A rotisserie bird is a plain chicken or a solution bird. A plain one is chicken with salt and spices, roasted in the store. A solution bird was pumped with a seasoning solution before the spit. The sticker says which.
entries.detail: Two label rules do the work. 9 CFR 381.117(h): a raw poultry product with added solution must carry a descriptive designation stating the percentage of added solution as a number with the % sign, e.g. ‘contains 15% added solution of water and salt’, plus the common or usual name of every solution ingredient in descending order; the word ‘enhanced’ may not appear in the product name. 9 CFR 381.118(a): any poultry product fabricated from two or more ingredients lists them by common or usual name in descending order of predominance; ingredients at 2 percent or less may trail the list under a ‘contains 2% or less of’ line. 9 CFR 424.21 permits sodium and potassium phosphates in poultry ‘to decrease the amount of cooked out juices’, capped at 0.5 percent of total product, and sodium hydroxide only alongside phosphate at one part to four. FSIS’s labeling glossary defines a bone-in bird injected or marinated with broth, water, fat or flavor enhancers as ‘basted’ or ‘self basted’, about 3 percent solution, with the solution ingredients named on the label. At the shelf the two kinds read differently: a plain bird’s panel is one line (Whole Foods Market’s organic rotisserie chicken lists ‘organic chicken’ and nothing else); a solution bird lists water and its seasoning after the chicken, in descending order as 381.118 requires; a phosphate, a starch and a sweetener are the usual entries. On the sticker, the second word on the list settles it: ‘salt’ or ‘spices’ is a plain bird; ‘water’ followed by ‘sodium phosphate’, ‘modified food starch’, ‘sugar’ is a solution bird, roasted. Both are cooked chicken. One of them is also a marinade injection.
sources: 9 CFR § 381.117 Name of product and other labeling (law.cornell.edu) https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/9/381.117
9 CFR § 424.21 Use of food ingredients and sources of radiation (law.cornell.edu) https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/9/424.21
USDA FSIS, Chicken from Farm to Table, Ready-Prepared Chicken https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/poultry/chicken-farm-table
USDA FSIS, Meat and Poultry Labeling Terms, Basted / Self basted https://www.fsis.usda.gov/food-safety/safe-food-handling-and-preparation/food-safety-basics/meat-and-poultry-labeling-terms

Whole Foods Market Organic Rotisserie Chicken, ingredient list from the package (EWG Food Scores, UPC 099482803568) https://www.ewg.org/foodscores/products/099482803568-WholeFoodsMarketOrganicRotisserieChicken/
entries.kristy_take: A roasted chicken should list a chicken. When the list runs to phosphate and starch, the seasoning went in with a needle.
entries.instead: A plain raw bird from the case, roasted at home. Salt it the night before; the skin does the rest.
buying_tips: Read the sticker, not the name. ‘Seasoned’, ‘original’ and ‘traditional’ are marketing; the ingredient list is regulated.
The shortest list wins: chicken, salt, spices. Water as the second ingredient means a solution was added.
Sodium phosphate, a starch or a sweetener after the water means a solution bird. The shorter the seasoning line, the plainer the chicken.
A bird held under the lamp is held hot for a reason. Take one that is steaming, not one that has sat.
watch_out: FSIS: eat or refrigerate a hot rotisserie bird within 2 hours of purchase. If it will not be eaten in that window, cut it up. Refrigerate it in shallow covered containers.
Hot food is held at or above 140°F. A bird sitting in the case long enough to fall below that has left its hold. FSIS puts the growth range at 40 to 140°F.
Eat within 3 to 4 days, cold or reheated to 165°F. Freezing is fine; use within 4 months for texture.

labels_decoded.meaning: Required wording under 9 CFR 381.117(h) for a raw bird with added solution: the percent as a number, then every solution ingredient in descending order. ‘Enhanced’ is not allowed in the product name.
FSIS term for a bone-in bird injected or marinated with broth, water, fat, spices or flavor enhancers, about 3 percent solution, with the ingredients named on the label.
A permitted poultry ingredient under 9 CFR 424.21 ‘to decrease the amount of cooked out juices’, capped at 0.5 percent of total product. On a rotisserie sticker it marks a solution bird.

entries.tier_note: Two federal label rules settle it; the ingredient list just needs reading.

entries.title: Beef cuts — what’s for what
entries.question: Which beef cut should I buy?
entries.decision: Chuck is the cut that falls apart when you cook it slowly.
entries.why: The hard-working cuts carry the connective tissue that melts into the broth.
entries.short_answer: Tougher, cheaper cuts like chuck, brisket and round want low-and-slow braising and stews. Tender cuts like ribeye, strip and tenderloin want quick high heat. The cheap cuts often have the most flavor if you cook them right.
entries.detail: Match the cut to the method. Muscles that work hard (shoulder/chuck, shank, round) are tougher and cheaper and turn tender with time and moisture. Muscles that don’t (loin, rib) are tender and pricier and want fast, hot cooking. Knowing this is how you eat well on a budget.
sources: USDA Institutional Meat Purchase Specifications (cut nomenclature)
Iowa State University Extension AnswerLine “Tender vs Less Tender Cuts of Meat” https://www.extension.iastate.edu/answerline/2016/06/09/tender-vs-less-tender-cuts-of-meat/
Flannery Beef “The Complete Guide to Beef Cuts” https://flannerybeef.com/blogs/news/the-complete-guide-to-beef-cuts
entries.kristy_take: Chuck roast and a slow cooker will out-eat a mediocre steak any day, for half the price.
buying_tips: Braise/stew: chuck, brisket, short rib, shank, round.
Quick sear/grill: ribeye, strip, sirloin, tenderloin.
Ground chuck (around 80/20) is the all-purpose workhorse.
entries.tier_note: Which cut earns the money is a cooking preference, held as a standard rather than dressed as fact.
watch_out: Tenderness comes from how hard the muscle worked and how much connective tissue it carries. It does not come from the age of the animal.
Chuck is shoulder and round is rear leg. Both are working muscles, less tender, and want liquid, low heat and time.
Loin and rib sit along the back and do little work, which is why they are the tender sections.
Marbling is the flecks of fat inside the muscle. More of it means a more tender, juicier steak once cooked, so look for it on a quick-cooked cut.
asked_as: which beef cut for stew
what cut of beef should i buy
cheap beef cut for slow cooking

entries.title: Ground beef lean ratios (80/20, 90/10)
entries.question: What ground beef lean ratio should I get?
entries.decision: 80/20 for burgers. 90/10 for anything you drain.
entries.why: The numbers are lean-to-fat by weight. It is a cooking choice, not a health one.
entries.short_answer: 80/20 is 20% fat, juicy and best for burgers. 90/10 is leaner, better for tacos, sauces or draining fat. Neither is ‘healthier’ in any way that matters much. Pick by what you’re cooking and your budget.
entries.detail: Fattier blends are cheaper and cook up juicier; leaner blends cost more and dry out faster. For dishes where you drain the fat anyway, a mid blend and a strainer gets you there for less. It’s a cooking-and-cost decision, not a health one.
entries.kristy_take: 80/20 for burgers, 90/10 when it is getting drained into a sauce. On a budget, buy 80/20 and drain it. Cheaper than lean.
buying_tips: 80/20: burgers, meatballs, anything where fat = flavor.
90/10: tacos, chili, sauces where you’d drain it.
‘Ground chuck/round/sirloin’ tells you the cut it came from.

labels_decoded.meaning: Lean % to fat % by weight — higher first number = leaner.

entries.tier_note: The ratio is a defined weight measure. What it changes is texture, which is cooking, not health.
asked_as: what ground beef should i buy
which ground beef for burgers
is 80/20 or 90/10 better
watch_out: ‘Ground beef’ may not have beef fat added as such; ‘hamburger’ may. Both cap at 30% fat, so the name is where the difference lives.
‘Ground beef’ may not contain added water, phosphates, binders or extenders. Its ingredient list should be beef, with seasoning at most.

entries.title: Egg labels, and what the hen ate
entries.question: What do cage-free, free-range, and pasture-raised eggs actually mean?
entries.decision: Soy-free and corn-free first, then organic, then pasture-raised.
entries.why: Space claims say nothing about the ration. A pasture-raised hen fed soy and corn is still a hen fed soy and corn.
entries.short_answer: Cage-free, free-range and pasture-raised are all space claims. None of them says what the hen ate. Most pasture-raised hens are still on soy and corn. The order that matters: soy-free and corn-free first, then organic, then pasture-raised.
entries.detail: ‘Soy-free’ and ‘corn-free’ have to be printed outright, because nothing else on the carton implies them, and most cartons never do. The claim clusters on small regional brands, farm stands and farmers markets rather than on the national pasture-raised labels, so the supermarket case is often the wrong place to look for it. Organic reaches the ration from a different direction: organic feed, no GMOs, no routine antibiotics, no added hormones. Pasture-raised paired with a third-party certification (Certified Humane, Animal Welfare Approved) is a real and audited claim about space, the strongest of the space words, and it still sits below feed here. Cage-free and free-range are weaker again, and the words on their own are not worth paying up for. Cage-free, free-range and pasture-raised describe how much room the hen had and whether she got outside, and not one of them says a word about what went in the trough. The order is what she ate, then how it was grown, then how much room she had.
sources: The Cornucopia Institute “Organic Egg Scorecard Criteria”, “Add On Labels” section https://www.cornucopia.org/egg-scorecard-criteria/
entries.kristy_take: Feed, then organic, then room. The space words are the ones everybody sells.
buying_tips: ‘Soy-free’ and ‘corn-free’ are the only words on the carton about the ration.
Organic reaches the feed from another direction: organic feed, no GMOs, no routine antibiotics.
‘Pasture-raised’ plus Certified Humane or Animal Welfare Approved is the strongest space claim.
Farm stands and farmers markets are where soy-free actually lives. Ask the person who keeps the hens.
Plain conventional eggs are still one of the cheapest complete proteins in the store.
watch_out: Most supermarket cartons never mention feed at all, the big pasture-raised brands included. Organic is the rung you can reliably buy there.
‘Vegetarian-fed’ means she was kept off animal protein. A hen on real pasture is eating bugs.
Yolk color is not a feed tell. Deep orange comes from a varied diet or from marigold in the ration, and the carton never says which.

Certified Humane is three different labels. Its pasture-raised tier sits well above its free-range tier. Its cage-free tier requires no outdoor access at all. The watchdog scores them 60, 50 and 30 on the same scale.
The labels the watchdog scores highest are Animal Welfare Approved, Biodynamic, Real Organic Project and Regenerative Organic Certified. A carton with no add-on label at all scores zero on that line.

labels_decoded.meaning: Not in cages — but usually still indoors, can be crowded.
Some outdoor access; the amount isn’t strictly defined.
Real pasture time — meaningful mainly when third-party certified.
A FEED claim — the only kind that addresses the ration. Must be printed explicitly.

entries.tier_note: What each carton word is allowed to mean is defined. Ranking feed above room is the standard.
asked_as: what eggs should i buy
which egg carton is best
which carton of eggs should i get

entries.title: Air-chilled chicken
entries.question: Is air-chilled chicken better?
entries.decision: Air-chilled is worth choosing; the other kind is cooled in a tank.
entries.why: Cold air instead of a communal tank. Nothing soaks in, and the skin starts dry.
entries.short_answer: Air-chilled birds are cooled in cold air. Water-chilled birds go through a communal chilled-water tank. They come out holding some of that water, and it is sold by the pound. The label has to print that number.
entries.detail: Conventional water-chilling can leave chicken holding added water (which you pay for by weight and which can dilute flavor). Air-chilling avoids that. Some people also prefer it on cross-contamination grounds, though safe handling matters far more than the chilling method. Retained water has to be disclosed on the label, so the number is printed rather than inferred. Skin that did not start out wet is also the skin that crisps.
sources: 9 CFR § 441.10 “Retained water in raw meat and poultry products” (Cornell LII) https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/9/441.10
entries.kristy_take: Air-chilled. Better skin, and nothing on the scale that is not chicken.
buying_tips: ‘Air-chilled’ is printed on the package when it applies.
A whole bird is the cheapest way to buy chicken either way.
Skin that starts dry is the skin that crisps.

labels_decoded.term: Contains up to X% retained water
labels_decoded.meaning: Water absorbed during water-chilling — you’re paying for it by weight.

entries.tier_note: Retained water is a disclosed number. Preferring air-chilled is a standard about handling.
watch_out: Water-chilled packages disclose ‘retained water up to’ a percentage. That percentage is the tank.
Where air-chilled is not stocked, a regular bird is still a clean cheap protein. Pat it dry before it goes in the pan.
No ‘retained water’ line on the label means none is allowed inside. The disclosure is required, not optional.
asked_as: what is air chilled chicken
is air chilled chicken better
which chicken should i buy

entries.title: ‘No antibiotics’ claims on chicken
entries.question: Does ‘no antibiotics’ on chicken mean anything?
entries.decision: Raised without antibiotics is a real claim, but not a cleaner bird.
entries.why: No chicken may be sold with residues either way. The claim is about how the flock was raised.
entries.short_answer: ‘Raised without antibiotics’ is a real claim, stated by the producer. Nobody inspects the farm to check it. No chicken can legally be sold with antibiotic residues anyway. The claim is about how the flock was raised, not residues.
entries.detail: US rules require a withdrawal period so meat is free of antibiotic residues regardless of the label. What ‘raised without antibiotics’ adds is information about flock management and antibiotic-resistance concerns. That is a legitimate reason to choose it, framed honestly. The claim itself is an affidavit, not an inspection, so look for USDA Process Verified or a third-party check to back it. The claim rests on the producer’s own paperwork to USDA. ‘No antibiotics’ isn’t as unique as it sounds. It speaks to how the flock was raised, not to residues on your plate.

entries.title: When organic produce is worth it
entries.question: Is organic produce worth the extra money?
entries.decision: Organic where the skin gets eaten. Conventional on anything peeled.
entries.why: Residue sits on the surface, so whatever gets thrown away takes it along.
entries.short_answer: Organic earns the money where the skin gets eaten: berries, leafy greens, apples, grapes, potatoes. Anything peeled goes in conventional, even the ones that feel delicate: avocado, kiwi, mango, banana, citrus, onion.
entries.detail: Pesticide residues on conventional produce are generally within legal limits, and washing removes some. The surface-residue reasoning is sound as a prioritization tool: the peel carries the exposure, so what gets discarded carries it away. The specific “Dirty Dozen” ranking and its risk framing are debated by scientists, so it rates a credible concern at most, never a settled fact. Eating more produce, organic or not, is the win. Avocado tests among the cleanest produce in the country. The part that was sprayed is the part that goes in the bin.
sources: peer-reviewed critiques of Dirty Dozen methodology
EWG Shopper's Guide to Pesticides in Produce (2025)
Environmental Working Group “Shopper’s Guide to Pesticides in Produce, full list” https://www.ewg.org/foodnews/full-list.php
entries.kristy_take: Spend it on the ones eaten whole. Everything that gets peeled, buy plain.
buying_tips: Ask one question at the shelf: does the skin get eaten? Berries, greens, apples, grapes and potatoes, yes. That is where the money goes.
Anything peeled goes in plain, however soft it looks. Avocado, kiwi, mango, banana, citrus and onion all test low.
Soak the conventional eaten-whole ones. A baking soda soak takes more surface residue off than a rinse.
watch_out: The rule is the SKIN, not how thick it feels. Avocado and kiwi read as delicate and get peeled, so they sit on the plain side. A potato reads as sturdy and gets eaten skin-on, so it does not.
Sturdy vegetables eaten whole are the gap this rule does not cover. Asparagus, cabbage, cauliflower, mushrooms and carrots test low anyway, so nothing is lost buying those plain.
Organic is not pesticide-free. It is a different approved list: copper, spinosad and pyrethrins are all permitted organic pesticides. The claim is fewer synthetic residues, never none.
The “Dirty Dozen” ranking is contested on its methodology. The eaten-whole reasoning holds; the list order does not.
If organic means fewer vegetables in the cart, buy conventional and eat more.
pick_steps: Ask if the skin gets eaten: berries, greens, apples, grapes, potatoes go organic.
Anything peeled goes in plain, however soft it feels, like avocado or kiwi.
Trust the USDA Organic seal; Natural means nothing on produce.
entries.science: Residue sits on the surface, so the part that gets peeled takes it away. A potato is eaten skin-on, so it counts; sturdy vegetables like cabbage and carrots test low anyway. Organic is not pesticide-free, just a different approved list with fewer synthetic residues. The Dirty Dozen order is contested; the eaten-whole reasoning holds. If organic means fewer vegetables, buy conventional and eat more.

labels_decoded.meaning: Grown to the National Organic Program rules and certified, with no SYNTHETIC pesticides. Not pesticide-free: copper, spinosad and pyrethrins are approved organic ones.

entries.title: Frozen vs. fresh produce
entries.question: Is frozen produce as good as fresh?
entries.decision: Frozen vegetables are picked ripe and frozen within hours.
entries.why: Picked ripe and frozen fast. ‘Fresh’ can lose more over days in transit.
entries.short_answer: Often just as good, sometimes better. Frozen is picked and frozen at peak ripeness, which locks in nutrients. ‘Fresh’ that travels a long way or sits in storage can lose some. Frozen does not spoil.
entries.detail: Studies comparing frozen and fresh find them broadly comparable in nutrition, with frozen sometimes ahead for produce that traveled far. Freezing is just cold, with no additives needed (check the bag is single-ingredient). This is established and it’s a genuine budget and waste win. Frozen fruit and vegetables do not spoil, and they are one of the better budget moves in the store.
sources: South Dakota State University Extension “Fresh May Not Always Be Best” https://extension.sdstate.edu/fresh-may-not-always-be-best

buying_tips: Check the bag lists just the vegetable/fruit. No sauces or added sugar.
Frozen berries and spinach are staples that never spoil.
Great for smoothies, soups, and sheet-pan roasts.
watch_out: ‘Fresh’ produce that traveled a long way or sat in storage can lose nutrients over time.
The advantage is picking and freezing at peak ripeness. ‘Fresh’ is not always best.

entries.title: Freezing what is about to turn
entries.question: How do I freeze produce before it goes off?
entries.decision: Enzymes keep working in the freezer until heat switches them off.
entries.why: Enzymes keep working below freezing and turn color and flavor. A brief scald ends them.
entries.short_answer: Freezing slows a vegetable down. It does not switch it off. The enzymes behind ripening and browning keep working in the freezer, slowly. Sixty seconds in boiling water switches them off.
entries.detail: Unblanched, a bag of beans comes out gray and tasting of hay months later, because the enzymes kept working. After the scald, the job is keeping air and ice crystals away from the food. Fruit is the exception and it is a real one: the enzymes that matter in fruit mostly affect appearance rather than flavor, and blanching would cook the texture out, so berries, banana and stone fruit go in raw. For vegetables the sequence is scald, chill hard in ice water to stop the cooking, dry, then freeze in a single layer before bagging. A tray first keeps the pieces separate instead of fusing into one brick you have to break with a knife. Air is the other enemy: what is called freezer burn is water subliming off the surface and leaving it dried and oxidised, and pressing the air out of the bag is most of the defense. Very high-water vegetables collapse whatever you do.
entries.kristy_take: Sixty seconds in boiling water, then ice, then a tray. That is the whole method.
sources: food-preservation guidance on enzyme inactivation and blanching times
work on sublimation and surface oxidation in frozen storage
buying_tips: Sixty seconds in boiling water, then straight into ice water to stop the cooking.
Freeze it flat on a tray before bagging, or it fuses into one brick.
Press the air out of the bag. Air is what burns it.
Fruit needs no blanching. Berries, banana and stone fruit go in as they are.
Date the bag. Frozen is not indefinite.
watch_out: Freezing rescues nothing that has already started to turn. It holds what you put in.
High-water vegetables collapse on thawing: cucumber, lettuce, radish. Those are not freezer candidates.
pick_steps: Scald vegetables sixty seconds, then plunge them into ice water.
Dry them, freeze flat on a tray, then bag with the air pressed out.
Fruit goes in raw; date every bag.
entries.science: Enzymes keep working below freezing, so unblanched beans come out gray and tasting of hay. A brief scald ends them. Fruit skips it, since blanching would cook the texture out. Air dries and oxidizes the surface, which is freezer burn. Freezing holds what goes in and rescues nothing already turning. High-water vegetables like cucumber, lettuce and radish collapse on thawing.
entries.tier_note: That enzymes survive freezing and a brief scald denatures them is settled food preservation science. It is also the step almost every home freeze skips.

entries.title: Buying produce in season
entries.question: Does buying produce in season matter?
entries.decision: Produce in season is picked closer to ripe and travels less.
entries.why: Abundance is the season showing. Out of season, frozen beats a pale expensive fresh.
entries.short_answer: For taste and price, yes. In-season produce is cheaper, more abundant, and usually tastes better because it didn’t travel as far. Out of season, frozen is often the smarter buy than a pale, expensive ‘fresh’ version.
entries.detail: Seasonality mostly affects flavor, cost, and freshness rather than making a food dramatically more nutritious. Off-season, produce is shipped long distances or grown under conditions that trade flavor for availability. That is exactly when frozen shines. The cheapest, most abundant thing in the department this week is almost always the seasonal one, so the price tag answers this before any chart does. Broadly: tender greens and berries in spring, tomatoes and stone fruit in summer, squash and apples in autumn, citrus and hardy brassicas in winter. The season-by-season list is below. Season shows up in the price and the size of the pile before it shows up anywhere else, so the cheapest, most abundant item in the department this week is usually the seasonal one. Some produce ignores the calendar because it stores well (apples, onions, potatoes, winter squash, carrots) or because it was shipped from the other hemisphere, which is why ‘available’ and ‘in season’ are different words. Citrus peaking in the dead of winter surprises people, and it is why a January orange tastes better than a July one. Whatever is piled high and cheap this week is what is in season. The price tag says it before any chart does.
sources: USDA Agricultural Marketing Service shipping-point season data
Michigan State University Extension “A How-To Guide to Eating for the Season” https://www.canr.msu.edu/news/a_how_to_guide_to_eating_for_the_season
entries.kristy_take: Buy the vegetables that are cheap and piled high this week. That’s what’s in season, and it’s where your money goes furthest.
buying_tips: The cheapest, most abundant produce this week is usually what’s in season.
Off-season, reach for frozen instead of sad ‘fresh’.
Farmers’ markets are a fast read on what’s actually in season locally.
Spring: asparagus, peas, radishes, artichokes, strawberries, tender greens.
Summer: tomatoes, corn, zucchini, peppers, cucumbers, stone fruit, melon, berries.
Autumn: winter squash, sweet potatoes, apples, pears, brussels sprouts, grapes.
Winter: citrus, cabbage, kale, leeks, beets, parsnips, storage onions and potatoes.
Storage crops (apples, onions, potatoes, squash, carrots) stay good long past their season.
watch_out: Summer has the most variety and some of it is only there for a short time. Strawberries come first, then cherries, blueberries, blackberries and raspberries, then peaches, melons, plums and pears.
To find what is in season near you, a farmers market or LocalHarvest is the direct route.
pick_steps: Take what is piled high and cheapest this week; that is the season.
Off-season, reach for frozen over a pale, sad fresh version.
Check a farmers market or LocalHarvest for what is in season near you.

Autumn brings squash and apples, winter citrus and hardy brassicas. Summer runs strawberries first, then cherries and other berries, then peaches, melons, plums and pears. Storage crops like apples, onions, potatoes and carrots stay good long past their season.
entries.tier_note: Reading the season off the market table is a shopping habit held as a standard, not a nutrition claim.

entries.title: Washing produce
entries.question: How should I wash produce?
entries.decision: Plain cold water removes as much residue as a produce wash does.
entries.why: Plain water is the recommendation. Rinse right before eating, not before storing.
entries.short_answer: Plain cold running water and a little rubbing is enough. No soap, no special produce wash. Rinse right before you eat, not before you store. Scrub firm produce with a brush; rinse and spin leafy greens.
entries.detail: Water and friction remove most surface dirt, microbes, and some residue. Soap and commercial washes aren’t recommended and aren’t proven better. Don’t wash berries or mushrooms until you’re ready to use them. Moisture speeds spoilage.
entries.kristy_take: Cold water and your hands. Skip the pricey ‘veggie wash’. It’s a solution to a problem you don’t have.
buying_tips: Rinse under cold running water; rub firm produce or use a brush.
Wash right before eating, not before storing (moisture = mold).
No soap or bleach. Plain water is the recommendation.
entries.tier_note: A plain-water rinse is the settled published recommendation; the bottled produce washes are not.
watch_out: Water is for dirt, not residue. If pesticide residue is the question, that is a twelve-minute baking soda soak.
pick_steps: Rinse under cold running water; brush firm produce, rinse and spin greens.
Wash right before eating, not before storing.
Skip soap, bleach and produce washes; plain water is the recommendation.
entries.science: Water and friction remove most surface dirt, microbes and some residue. Soap and commercial washes are not recommended and are not proven better. Moisture speeds spoilage, so berries and mushrooms stay dry until use. Water is for dirt, not residue. Residue is the job of a twelve-minute baking soda soak.

entries.title: Getting residue off conventional produce
entries.question: Does washing actually get the pesticide residue off?
entries.decision: Baking soda in the water lifts residue a plain rinse leaves.
entries.why: A rinse moves dirt. Bicarbonate breaks residue down, and it needs minutes to do it.
entries.short_answer: Baking soda breaks down some pesticide residues on the skin. Running water mostly moves them around. It takes twelve to fifteen minutes in the bowl, not thirty seconds under the tap. Residue already in the flesh stays.
entries.detail: A soak does what a rinse cannot. Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate, and it degrades some residues on the skin, where running water mostly relocates them. It is a surface treatment and only a surface treatment. The study everyone is quoting applied two pesticides to organic Gala apples and compared tap water, a one percent baking soda solution, and the bleach solution used commercially. Baking soda came out ahead of both, removing most of the surface phosmet at twelve minutes and most of the surface thiabendazole at fifteen. The same work is where the limit comes from: thiabendazole was mapped eighty micrometers into the fruit and phosmet twenty, and nothing applied to the outside reaches that. A later comparison across apples, grapes, lemons and strawberries put baking soda alone lower and found a commercial product ahead of it, so the honest position is that the soak beats water and the ranking against bottled washes is not settled.
sources: Yang et al. 2017, J. Agric. Food Chem. — baking soda vs tap water vs a commercial bleach solution, on lab-dosed organic apples
2025 comparison of household and commercial washing agents across apples, grapes, lemons and strawberries
entries.kristy_take: A rinse is for dirt. If residue is the reason, it is a soak and it takes twelve minutes.
buying_tips: A teaspoon of baking soda per two cups of water, enough to cover the fruit.
Twelve to fifteen minutes in the bowl. Thirty seconds under the tap is not the same thing.
Worth the trouble on thin-skinned conventional fruit you eat whole: apples, grapes, berries.
Rinse the soda off with plain water afterward.
watch_out: Systemic pesticides do not come off. Thiabendazole was mapped eighty micrometers into the apple, and no surface treatment reaches that.
Peeling removes more than any soak, and it removes the peel with it.
The circulating ‘ninety percent of pesticides’ line overstates the study. Two compounds were measured, on apples the researchers had dosed themselves.
pick_steps: A teaspoon of baking soda per two cups of water, covering the fruit.
Soak twelve to fifteen minutes, then rinse the soda off with plain water.
Use it on thin-skinned conventional fruit eaten whole: apples, grapes, berries.
entries.science: Baking soda degrades some skin residues, where running water mostly moves them around. It needs minutes, not thirty seconds under the tap. Systemic residue stays: thiabendazole was mapped eighty micrometers into the apple. Peeling removes more than any soak, and the peel goes with it. The ‘ninety percent’ line overstates one study: two compounds, applied by the researchers to apples.
entries.tier_note: Surface residue is a credible peer-reviewed concern, and the twelve-minute soak comes from one study whose numbers are not settled.

entries.title: Pre-cut and pre-washed produce
entries.question: Is pre-cut produce a good buy?
entries.decision: Cutting produce starts the clock on vitamin loss and browning.
entries.why: Cutting opens every surface at once. It costs more and it keeps for days, not weeks.
entries.short_answer: Cutting produce starts the clock. Pre-cut and bagged costs more per pound. It gives up what whole produce does best: waiting until the day you need it. Nutrient loss from cutting is minor and measured. Spoilage is the real cost.
entries.detail: Cutting exposes more surface to air and light, so pre-cut produce loses a little more nutrition and freshness over time and carries a small extra food-safety consideration. Rinse bagged greens even if ‘pre-washed’. The real cost is price and a shorter fridge life. For a short-on-time week, that can be exactly the right call.

entries.kristy_take: Buy it whole and cut it yourself. Two minutes, and it keeps a week longer.
buying_tips: Whole produce is cheaper per pound and keeps far longer.
Use pre-cut within a couple of days. It spoils fast once opened.
Give ‘pre-washed’ greens a rinse anyway.

watch_out: If a bag of pre-washed greens is the difference between a salad and no salad, buy the bag. Eaten beats perfect.
Pre-cut melon and pineapple sit closest to the edge. Buy those the day you eat them.
Whole skin protects the fruit. Sliced and chopped produce has more exposed surface and supports microbial growth more easily. Low-acid items that grew touching dirt, melon first, need the most care.
‘Sell by’, ‘use by’ and ‘best by’ on a tub are not regulated. They are how the company chose to present the product, not a safety cutoff.

Buy pre-cut melon and pineapple the day they get eaten.
If the bag is what makes the salad happen, buy the bag.

Whole skin protects the fruit; cut produce supports microbial growth more easily, melon most of all. Sell-by and use-by dates on a tub are not regulated, and they are not a safety cutoff.

entries.title: Grass-fed butter
entries.question: Is grass-fed butter worth it?
entries.decision: Butter from cows on grass carries more omega-3 than grain-fed.
entries.why: Carotene from the grass goes into the fat. The fatty-acid profile shifts with it.
entries.short_answer: Cows on grass eat carotene, and it goes straight into the fat. So grass-fed butter runs deep yellow toward orange. Winter butter from the same dairy runs pale. The fat itself shifts modestly too.
entries.detail: Butter is cream, and salt if it is salted. A tub spread is a formulation: vegetable or seed oils, water, emulsifiers and flavoring, built to behave like butter and to cost less. Within real butter, the grass difference is a feed difference showing up three ways at once: in the color, in the fat, and on the tongue. European-style butters are churned to a higher fat content, which is a separate axis from what the cows ate and the reason they bake and finish differently. The taste and the way it behaves in a hot pan are differences people can actually pick out, which is more than most sourcing claims manage. The fatty-acid profile shifts modestly too.
entries.kristy_take: The deep yellow is the grass. Winter butter from the same dairy goes pale.
buying_tips: Deep yellow toward orange is carotene from grass. Pale is a hay-fed winter churn.
European-style butters are higher in fat, a separate axis from what the cows ate.
Salted or unsalted is a cooking choice. Unsalted gives control.

entries.tier_note: The color and the fat both shift measurably with the diet. Paying up for them is the standard.
watch_out: A tub spread is not butter. It is oils, water and emulsifiers built to behave like it, and the list says so.
‘Spreadable butter’ is butter cut with canola or olive oil. The ingredient list says which.
Color tracks the season as well as the standard. The same dairy churns paler in winter.

entries.title: Whole vs. reduced-fat milk
entries.question: Should I buy whole or low-fat milk?
entries.decision: Whole milk is intact; reduced-fat has had the cream spun out.
entries.why: Skim is whole milk with the fat taken out. Fewer steps is the standard here.
entries.short_answer: Reduced-fat, low-fat and skim are all whole milk with milkfat removed. The fat carries the flavor and most of the fullness. Dairy fat research is mixed, so the call rests on the processing, the checkable part.
entries.detail: Whole milk is the one that had the least done to it. For years the guidance was ‘always low-fat dairy’, and the evidence behind that for otherwise-healthy people has weakened. Dairy fat is an area of honest debate, so whole milk is a whole-food-standard pick rather than a finding. What is not debated is the handling: skimming, standardizing and often ultra-pasteurizing are steps, and whole minimally-processed milk has fewer of them. A doctor’s advice for a specific person outranks a shelf standard. The old blanket advice to always choose low-fat dairy has softened, and the research on dairy fat is genuinely mixed.
sources: reviews of dairy-fat and cardiometabolic outcomes (contested literature)
Michigan State University Extension, dairy processing article (milk standardized to skim, 1%, 2% and whole through separators)
Florida Dairy Farmers “How Much Fat is in Whole Milk?” https://www.floridamilk.com/in-the-news/blog/nutrition/how-much-fat-is-in-whole-milk-whole-2-low-fat-and-skim-milk-explained.stml

buying_tips: Whole milk is 3.25% milkfat by federal standard. Reduced-fat is 2%, low-fat 1%, skim under half a percent.
Grass-fed and pasture milk is a further layer, and a separate question from the fat.
Cream-top means non-homogenized. The cream line is the visible version of fewer steps.
watch_out: Chocolate and strawberry jugs carry dessert-level added sugar. Check that line before the fat one.
Ultra-pasteurized whole milk is still a further step. A date months out is the tell.

entries.title: A2 vs. A1 milk
entries.question: Is A2 milk worth buying over regular milk?
entries.decision: A2 is worth choosing, and it suits people upset by ordinary milk.
entries.why: One amino acid apart, and only A1 releases the BCM-7 peptide. Sourcing still outranks it.
entries.short_answer: Worth choosing when the rest of the carton is equal. Jerseys, Guernseys and most heritage and older European breeds carry A2. Kristy prefers the older genetics. It sits below the herd and the processing, not above them.
entries.detail: The genetics are not in question: the A1 variant arose as a mutation in European herds and spread through the breeds selected hardest for volume, and the BCM-7 release is a straightforward consequence of where the amino acid sits in the chain. What is thin is everything downstream of that. The human studies on how A2 milk sits with people are small, inconsistent, and several were funded by the a2 Milk Company, which owns the branding and licenses the seal. So the honest position is a preference for the older genetics rather than a finding about what they do. A2 is also a marketing program, not only a breed trait. A2 milk from a confinement dairy is still a confinement dairy, and the seal says nothing about how the herd lived or how the milk was handled. The high-output Holstein herds that fill supermarket cartons skew A1.
sources: characterization of the A1 and A2 beta-casein variants and BCM-7 release in digestion
human digestive-comfort trials on A2 milk (small, inconsistent, several industry-funded)
University of Minnesota Extension “A2 milk and A2 genetics” https://extension.umn.edu/agriculture/animals-and-livestock/dairy/a2-milk-and-a2-genetics
entries.kristy_take: The older breeds, and one amino acid is the whole of it. Worth choosing. Not worth choosing first.
buying_tips: The ladder runs four steps. Raw from a farm you can name. Then low-temp pasteurized and cream-top. Then A2, then the carton in front of you.
Jersey and Guernsey are the A2 breeds. Small dairies name the breed; the big labels only print the seal.
People who struggle with regular milk often do better on A2. Worth trying for a week.
A2 yogurt and A2 cheese are the same milk cultured. The breed question does not change.
watch_out: Ultra-pasteurized A2 is still UHT. The A2 claim says nothing about processing, and processing is the higher-order question.
The seal is a licensed program, not a farming standard. It reports the protein and nothing about how the herd lived.

Easier to digest is the most promising claim and still the unproven one. The extension line says the digestion and health claims for A2 have not been proven by science. The label reports which protein is in the carton and nothing more.

Breed is a tendency, not a test. Jerseys and Guernseys carry more A2 genes than Holsteins. Still, a Holstein herd can be more than half A2A2. An A1A2 cow gives milk with both proteins. The claim rests on a tested herd, not on the breed.

entries.title: Real cheese, and why the block beats the bag
entries.question: Should I buy block cheese, slices, or pre-shredded?
entries.decision: Block cheese is milk, cultures, salt and enzymes, and nothing else.

entries.title: Rice and arsenic
entries.question: Should I buy white rice or brown?
entries.decision: Arsenic collects in the bran, which is why white rice carries less.
entries.why: Arsenic concentrates in the bran, and the bran is what brown rice keeps.
entries.short_answer: Rice takes up more arsenic from soil and water than other grains. The bran holds most of it. Brown rice tests about half again higher than white. Variety and origin matter more than color. White basmati is the strong pick.
entries.detail: Two testing programs put numbers on it. Consumer Reports measured brown rice at 113 ppb inorganic arsenic against white at 72; Healthy Babies Bright Futures measured 129 against 86. By variety, basmati averaged 55 ppb and sushi rice 57, while plain long-grain and parboiled both averaged 101. Origin moves it as much as color does. Rice grown in Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri and Texas tests highest, and California, India and Pakistan test lowest. Why the southern crop runs high is not settled. Those fields carry residue from decades of arsenical pesticides used on cotton, and the same fields also have sandier soil, which releases arsenic more readily than clay. Both explanations are published and neither has been shown to be the whole of it. Cooking is the other lever, and it is a large one: boiling rice in plenty of water and pouring the water off removes 40 to 60 percent of the inorganic arsenic, while rinsing and soaking were each measured at 5 percent or less. The FDA has set an action level of 100 ppb for infant rice cereal and has set nothing for table rice. Rice takes up more inorganic arsenic from soil and water than other grains. Brown rice tests about half again higher than white in every testing program that has looked.
sources: Consumer Reports, rice heavy-metals testing https://www.consumerreports.org/health/food-safety/arsenic-in-your-food-testing-shows-a-real-need-for-federal-standards-a1064475937/ (measurable inorganic arsenic in every sample tested; rinsing and soaking removed less than 8 percent, while the parboil-and-absorption method removed 50 to 58 percent)
Healthy Babies Bright Futures, What’s in Your Family’s Rice?, 2025

Zavala and Duxbury on arsenic in US rice by growing region
NIH Office of Dietary Supplements, food sources of magnesium
entries.kristy_take: Take the white basmati. Boil it in plenty of water and pour the water off. Rice was never where anybody got their minerals.

entries.title: Oats: steel-cut vs. rolled vs. instant
entries.question: What kind of oats should I buy?
entries.decision: Plain oats are the same grain in every form; packets add sugar.
entries.why: Same grain, cut differently. The packets are where the sugar is.

Steel-cut are the least processed (chewy, slow to cook, gentlest on blood sugar); rolled/old-fashioned are steamed and flattened (quick, versatile); instant are pre-cooked and often come pre-sweetened. The measured number is the glycemic index: 42 for steel-cut, 55 for rolled and 83 for instant, in one extension comparison.

entries.title: Salting the bean soak
entries.question: Does salting the soak water make beans tough?
entries.decision: Brining beans softens the skins; the old rule has it backwards.
entries.why: Sodium loosens what holds the bean’s skin together, so a salted soak leaves the skin softer.
entries.short_answer: Sodium in the soak loosens the bean’s skin rather than tightening it. So salted beans cook more evenly and blow out less. The rule against salting is old, widely repeated, and wrong about the mechanism.
entries.detail: Two different things got confused. Acid does firm a bean: tomato, vinegar, wine and molasses added early will keep skins tough for hours, which is why a pot of chili can sit at a stubborn crunch. Hard water does it too, because the calcium and magnesium in it cross-link the pectin. Salt does neither. It is the one common addition that moves the other way, and the folk rule appears to have collected all three effects under the one ingredient people add most. Age matters more than any of it: beans that have sat for years never fully soften, whatever is in the water. It is the opposite of the received wisdom. Sodium works its way into the seed coat and displaces the calcium and magnesium holding the pectin together, which weakens the skin rather than tightening it, so salted beans cook more evenly and blow out less.
entries.kristy_take: Salt the water. The rule your grandmother gave you was about the tomatoes.
sources: food-chemistry work on pectin cross-linking and cation exchange in legume seed coats
controlled kitchen testing of salted versus unsalted soaks
buying_tips: A heaped tablespoon of salt per quart of soaking water, overnight.
Salt the cooking water as well. The same softening applies while they simmer.
Buy from a bin that turns over. Old beans stay hard however you soak them.
watch_out: Acid genuinely does harden beans. Hold the tomato, vinegar and molasses until the skins are tender.
Hard tap water works against you: the calcium and magnesium in it do the opposite of what sodium does.
entries.tier_note: Salt in the soaking water is real food chemistry held as a standard, since its practical size comes from kitchen testing rather than settled study.

entries.title: “Cage-free” and “free-range”
entries.question: What do ‘cage-free’ and ‘free-range’ actually require?
entries.decision: Cage-free and free-range both describe a barn, not a field.
entries.why: Cage-free is a barn. Free-range adds a door, with the size and the hours left undefined.
entries.short_answer: Both are weaker than they sound. ‘Cage-free’ hens are out of cages but typically indoors in large barns, and can be crowded. ‘Free-range’ adds some outdoor access, loosely defined. For outdoor living, look for ‘pasture-raised’ with a third-party certification.
entries.detail: The two terms mark rungs on the same ladder and people routinely read both as a meadow. Cage-free is a defined term for eggs and a genuine welfare improvement on conventional cages; on products other than eggs it carries much less. Free-range signals outdoor access but sets a low, loosely-enforced bar with no certification required. Above both sits pasture-raised, which only means anything with a certifier attached: Certified Humane, Animal Welfare Approved, or Global Animal Partnership. Match the word to what you actually want rather than to the picture on the carton. ‘Cage-free’ is a real step up from battery cages, and not outdoors. entries.title: “Grass-fed” (the label)

entries.title: What “pasture-raised” does and does not tell you
aliases: are pasture raised eggs soy free
entries.question: Does “pasture-raised” mean the animal wasn’t fed soy and corn?
entries.decision: It means space, not feed. The word to find is soy-free.
entries.why: Cage-free, free-range and pasture-raised are room claims. Most of those hens still eat soy and corn.
entries.short_answer: No. Cage-free, free-range and pasture-raised all describe SPACE, not FEED. None says what went in the trough. Most pasture-raised hens are still fed soy and corn. If feed matters, look for a printed “soy-free”. Nothing else implies it.
entries.detail: USDA has no regulatory definition of “pasture-raised” at all; where it means something, it is because a third-party certifier defined it. Certified Humane, for instance, requires 108 square feet of outdoor space per hen. Those standards govern housing and outdoor access. They do not specify a ration. “Certified organic” is the one term that does reach feed, and it requires the feed be organic, which in practice is usually organic soy and organic corn. Organic answers how the feed was grown; it does not answer what the feed is. This is the single widest gap between what a carton implies and what it guarantees, and it is why two cartons with identical front-of-pack language can come from birds raised on completely different diets. These labels tell you how much room the animal had and whether it got outside. If feed is what you care about, the word to look for is “soy-free”; it has to be printed, because nothing else on the carton implies it.

entries.title: What “organic” covers — and what it doesn’t
entries.question: What does the organic seal actually guarantee?
entries.decision: Organic certifies how food was grown, not how processed it is.
entries.why: It covers inputs and practices, not nutrition or processing. It is not pesticide-free.
entries.short_answer: It is a production standard, not a quality rating. Certified organic means no prohibited synthetic pesticides, no GMOs, organic feed for animals, and no routine antibiotics or added hormones. It is not pesticide-free. An organic cookie is a cookie.
entries.detail: The National Organic Program defines organic as a set of permitted and prohibited INPUTS and practices, verified by certification. That is a real, enforced standard and worth something. What it is not is a nutrition claim: the seal is silent on whether the food is nutrient-dense or minimally processed, and ultra-processed foods can carry it in full compliance. Reading it as a shorthand for “good food” is the most common way it gets misused. Organic tells you how something was grown or raised, and you still have to look at what the thing actually is. Certified organic means no synthetic pesticides from the prohibited list. It does not mean pesticide-free (approved natural ones are allowed), and it makes no claim at all about nutrient density, how well an animal was raised beyond the baseline, or how processed the food is.
sources: USDA National Organic Program, 7 CFR Part 205 (permitted and prohibited substances)
USDA AMS organic labeling and certification requirements
entries.kristy_take: Organic tells you how it was grown, not what it is. The seal on a box of cookies is still a box of cookies.
buying_tips: Organic is about inputs and practices. Read the ingredient panel separately.

entries.title: Does the origin sticker matter?
entries.question: Does the country on the sticker tell me anything about quality?
entries.decision: Two pieces from the same bin can be weeks apart in ripeness.
entries.why: Origin tells you the season. Quality tracks ripeness, handling and time in transit.
entries.short_answer: The sticker is a calendar, not a grade. The same variety grows in several countries with different seasons, so the origin changes through the year. Quality tracks ripeness, handling and time in transit. The country shows none of that.
entries.detail: Avocados are the clearest example of the confusion. Hass is a VARIETY, and it is grown in California, Mexico, Peru and elsewhere; the growing regions have different seasons, which is why the origin sticker changes through the year. That is a calendar difference, not a quality ranking. Ranking one country over another on a produce sticker is a habit worth dropping, because the piece in your hand is the only thing that answers the question. Where origin does earn attention is transit time: something grown closer was picked closer to ripe, which is a handling argument rather than a country one. Learn the checks for the specific item and any bin can be picked well.
sources: USDA produce grading and handling standards
University extension produce selection and ripening guidance

entries.title: “Multigrain” vs. “whole grain”
entries.question: Is multigrain bread whole grain?
entries.decision: ‘Multigrain’ counts grains; ‘whole grain’ says the bran stayed in.
entries.why: Multigrain allows every grain to be refined. Whole grain means the kernel is intact.
entries.short_answer: Not necessarily, and usually not. “Multigrain” only means more than one grain is in there. Every one of them can be refined. “Whole grain” means the kernel is intact, bran and germ included.
entries.detail: Neither term is a grading claim, but “whole grain” has a defined meaning tied to the intact kernel, while “multigrain” is a count. A loaf can be multigrain, seven-grain, or stone-ground and still be built on refined flour. The reliable read is the ingredient panel: a whole grain should be the FIRST ingredient, and “100% whole grain” on the front is stronger than “made with whole grains”, which permits any fraction. Color tells you nothing. Brown bread is frequently white flour with caramel coloring. “Whole grain” means the kernel is intact: bran, germ and endosperm. They are answers to different questions, and only one of them is about refinement.
entries.kristy_take: “Multigrain” is a headcount, not a standard. Seven refined grains is still seven refined grains. Turn it over: a whole grain has to be the first ingredient, or the front of the bag is decoration.
buying_tips: Read the first ingredient. “Whole wheat flour” counts; “wheat flour” and “enriched flour” do not.
“100% whole grain” is a real claim. “Made with whole grains” permits any fraction.
Ignore the color. Brown can be caramel coloring on white flour.

entries.title: “Lightly sweetened” and the sugar words
entries.question: Does “lightly sweetened” mean anything?
entries.decision: ‘Lightly sweetened’ is not defined, so the number is the only answer.
entries.why: ‘Lightly sweetened’ has no definition. The panel number is the one that cannot be spun.
entries.short_answer: No. It has no standardized definition. Neighboring terms do: “no sugar added” means none was added during processing. “Reduced sugar” means at least 25% less than a reference product. Only the added-sugar line on the panel cannot be spun.
entries.detail: This is a case where the regulated and the unregulated sit side by side on the same package. “Lightly sweetened” is not a defined claim. “No sugar added” and “reduced sugar” are defined, but neither means low: a juice with no added sugar is still concentrated fruit sugar, and 25% less than something very sweet is still sweet. Since added sugars became a separate line on the Nutrition Facts panel, the fastest honest read is to skip the front of the package entirely and look at that number, then check the ingredient list for the aliases: cane juice, syrups, concentrates. ‘Lightly sweetened’ is worth exactly what the marketing department decided it was worth. “No sugar added” leaves the food’s own sugars, and “reduced sugar” can still be a lot.
sources: FDA 21 CFR 101.60 (nutrient content claims for sugars)
FDA Nutrition Facts label final rule — added sugars declaration
entries.kristy_take: “Lightly sweetened” isn’t a standard, it’s an adjective. The added-sugar line is right there on the back and nobody gets to negotiate with it.

“No sugar added” still allows the food’s own sugars, which can be substantial.

entries.title: “No artificial flavors” — what still gets in
entries.question: If it says no artificial flavors, what is the flavoring?
entries.decision: The claim bans synthetic flavoring but leaves everything else untouched.
entries.why: Natural flavors are still engineered. The legal difference is the starting material.
entries.short_answer: Natural flavors, still permitted and still made in a lab. The legal difference is the source material, not the processing. Natural flavors must start from a plant or animal. Either can be dozens of substances declared as two words.
entries.detail: The definition sits in 21 CFR 101.22: a natural flavor is derived from a spice, fruit, vegetable, edible yeast, herb, bark, bud, root, leaf, meat, seafood, egg or dairy product, whose significant function is flavoring. That is a rule about origin. It permits substantial processing, and it permits incidental additives (solvents, preservatives and carriers) to ride along inside the blend without separate declaration. So “no artificial flavors” is a true statement that answers a narrower question than most people think they are asking. The objection is the opacity rather than the word “artificial”: either way, two words on a panel stand in for a formulation nobody can see. A natural flavor has to start from something plant or animal derived; an artificial one does not. Both arrive as engineered compounds, and either can be a proprietary blend of dozens of substances declared as two words on the panel.
sources: FDA 21 CFR 101.22 (definitions of natural and artificial flavor)
FDA guidance on incidental additives in flavor formulations
entries.kristy_take: “No artificial flavors” only rules out one kind of lab work. Natural flavoring is still a formulation, and it can be dozens of compounds hiding behind two words. That’s an opacity problem, not a chemistry one.
buying_tips: The claim rules out artificial flavoring only. Natural flavoring is still permitted.
Both are engineered; the legal difference is the starting material, not the process.
“Natural flavors” can carry solvents and carriers that need no separate declaration.

entries.title: Egg color — shell and yolk
entries.question: Do brown shells or darker yolks mean a better egg?
entries.decision: Shell color is breed; yolk color is pigment in the feed.
entries.why: Shell color is the breed. Yolk color is pigment in the feed, and an additive matches a good diet exactly.
entries.short_answer: No, on both counts. Shell color is the breed. Inside, white and brown are the same egg. Yolk color is pigment in the feed. A varied diet deepens it, and so does added marigold extract. The two look identical.
entries.detail: Shell color is pigment the hen deposits in the last hours before laying, and it tracks breed. Brown often costs more because those breeds are larger and eat more, not because the egg is better. Yolk color is the more tempting signal and the more misleading one: producers can and do dial it with feed, and the supplements sold to do it are sold for exactly that purpose. Pasture and varied diets deepen color too, which is what makes it useless: the same shade arrives by two completely different routes and the carton never says which. What actually changes an egg is the hen’s diet, her age, and how fresh it is, and none of it is visible from outside. White-feathered breeds lay white, red-feathered breeds lay brown, and inside the shell they are the same egg. A varied diet with real greens deepens yolk color, and so does marigold extract added to the ration for that exact effect. The two are indistinguishable by eye. That is why the printed feed words are the tell and the color never is. Blue and green shells carry a different pigment, biliverdin, laid down by breeds like the Araucana.
sources: USDA Egg Grading Manual (shell color and breed)
entries.kristy_take: Shell color is the breed and yolk color is the feed bag. Buy the cheaper carton and put the difference into how she was raised.
buying_tips: Ignore shell color. It says nothing about the egg inside.
A varied diet deepens yolk color. So does an additive bought to do it.
Speckles and small rough patches are normal shell variation.
Freshness shows in the pan: a yolk that stands up, a white that holds together.

entries.title: How fresh is that carton
entries.question: How do I tell how fresh eggs are?
entries.decision: The three-digit code is the day the eggs were packed.
entries.why: The three-digit date beside the plant code is the day it was packed. Sell-by is the store’s schedule.
entries.short_answer: Read the three-digit pack date, not the sell-by. It sits beside the plant code: the day the eggs were packed. Eggs are usually good well past a sell-by if they stayed cold. Fresh yolks stand up in the pan.
entries.detail: The Julian pack date is the honest number: 001 is January 1st, 365 is December 31st. A sell-by sits up to 45 days past packing and is a store-rotation instruction, not a safety cliff. The float test works because the air cell inside grows as an egg ages, so a fresh one lies flat in a bowl of water, an older one tilts up, and one that floats has gone far enough to skip. Eggs age much faster on the counter than in the fridge. US cartons carry a Julian date (001 to 365) stamped beside the plant code, and that is the day they were packed. In the pan, a fresh egg has a yolk that stands up and a white that holds together.
sources: USDA FSIS shell-egg dating and Julian pack codes
USDA Egg Grading Manual (air cell and interior quality)

University of Nebraska–Lincoln Extension “Cracking the Date Code on Egg Cartons” https://food.unl.edu/article/cracking-date-code-egg-cartons/ (Julian pack date; eggs keep 4 to 5 weeks past the pack date refrigerated)

Open the carton and check for cracks and leaks before it goes in the cart.
Float test at home: flat on the bottom is fresh, standing on end is old, floating goes out.
A fresh egg fries with a tall yolk and a tight white. A flat, spreading one is old, not unsafe.

entries.title: Egg grades and sizes
entries.question: What do egg grades and sizes actually mean?
entries.decision: Grade and size describe the egg’s looks and weight, not the hen.
entries.why: Grade scores appearance, size is weight per dozen. Recipes assume Large.
entries.short_answer: Grade scores appearance and interior quality, not nutrition or welfare. AA has the firmest white and tallest yolk, A a step down. B is fine to eat and mostly goes to processing. Size is weight per dozen. Recipes assume Large.
entries.detail: Graders score the shell, the air cell, and how the white and yolk sit when the egg is broken out. AA and A differ only in how firm the white is, and firmness fades with age anyway, so a Grade A egg packed yesterday beats an AA packed a month ago. Size is set by the weight of a full dozen, so a Jumbo carton is not a better egg, it is more egg. Comparing price per ounce rather than per dozen is usually where the value turns up. Size is pure weight per dozen: Large is 24 ounces, Extra Large 27, Jumbo 30.
