entries.title: Why US eggs live in the fridge
entries.question: Do eggs have to be refrigerated?
entries.decision: Washing strips the shell’s natural coating, so US eggs need the fridge.
entries.why: Washing strips the natural coating that seals a porous shell. Unwashed farm eggs keep theirs.
entries.short_answer: In the US, yes. Eggs sold here are washed at the plant. Washing strips the natural coating that seals a porous shell. After that, the egg needs constant refrigeration. Unwashed farm eggs keep the coating and can sit out.
entries.detail: US rules require washing and sanitizing, then holding at 45F or below from the plant onward. Neither system is wrong; they solve the same problem from opposite ends. In the carton on a middle shelf is the right spot, not the door, where the temperature swings every time it opens. A cold egg brought to room temperature sweats, and moisture on a porous shell is exactly what the cuticle was preventing. Farm eggs bought unwashed can live on the counter, but the moment you wash them they join the fridge rules. Washing strips the cuticle, the natural coating that seals a porous shell. Unwashed farm eggs keep their cuticle and can sit out, which is why cartons sit on an open shelf across much of Europe. What you should not do is move an egg between the two.
sources: USDA FSIS shell egg refrigeration requirements (45F)
EU marketing standards for eggs (unwashed, ambient storage)
entries.kristy_take: Washed eggs lost their seal, so they live cold. Unwashed farm eggs kept theirs, so they do not. Just do not switch an egg between the two.
buying_tips: Store the carton on a middle shelf, not the door. The door swings warm every time it opens.
Keep them in the carton. It slows moisture loss and keeps odors out.
Unwashed farm eggs can stay on the counter. Once washed, they need the fridge for good.
Leftover raw whites and yolks keep a few days covered. Yolks want a little water over them.

labels_decoded.meaning: The US standard. The cuticle is gone, so refrigeration is required.
Cuticle intact. Can be held at room temperature until washed.

entries.tier_note: That washing strips the cuticle is established, and it is why washed eggs need the cold.
watch_out: A cold egg left out at room temperature can sweat. Moisture on the shell is where bacteria can take hold. Refrigerated eggs should not sit out more than two hours.
Keep the carton on a middle or lower shelf, not the door. The door swings warm every time it opens.
Store-bought eggs do not need washing before use. They were already washed and sanitized at the plant.

entries.title: USDA beef grades: Prime, Choice, Select
entries.question: What do Prime, Choice and Select mean?
entries.decision: Grade is a marbling score, and marbling only shows in fast cooking.
entries.why: Grade measures marbling and age. It says nothing about how the animal was raised.
entries.short_answer: Grade scores marbling, the fat inside the muscle, and age. Prime has the most, Choice is the usual middle grade, Select is leanest and driest. It says nothing about how the animal was raised, fed, or whether it got outside.
entries.detail: Grade is a cooking and eating-quality scale, and marbling is the fat threaded inside the muscle. Grading is voluntary and paid for by the packer, so plenty of good beef carries no grade at all, including much grass-finished beef, whose marbling pattern the scale was not built around. Marbling melts during cooking, which is why a Prime steak forgives high heat and a Select one dries out. On a braising cut the grade matters far less, because time and moisture do the work the fat would have done. Grade and sourcing are two separate axes, and neither implies the other.

buying_tips: Prime, Choice, Select is a marbling scale, top to bottom.
Grading is voluntary. Ungraded is not a downgrade, and a lot of grass-finished beef skips it.
Pay up for grade on a quick-cooked steak. Skip it on anything braised.
Grade and sourcing are separate questions. Neither answers the other.

entries.title: Judging meat at the case
aliases: how to tell if meat is fresh
entries.question: How do I tell good meat from the case?
entries.decision: Color comes from oxygen and packaging, not from how fresh it is.
entries.why: Color is oxygen. A sealed package that is not leaking, and no off smell, tell you more.
entries.short_answer: Color is the least useful signal, yet everybody uses it. Bright red beef has met oxygen; purple-red vacuum-packed beef has not. Both are fine. Better checks: a sealed package with no leaks, fine marbling, no off smell or slime.
entries.detail: Beef pigment turns bright red within minutes of oxygen exposure and oxidizes browner over days. That is surface chemistry, not spoilage, which is why a vacuum-sealed roast looks purple and a freshly cut steak looks cherry-red. The liquid in a tray is called purge; the check is the package itself, fully sealed, with no holes, tears or punctures, and not leaking meat juices. Marbling should run through the muscle in fine threads; a thick outer fat cap is trim, not marbling. Sell-by dates are set by the store. Trust your nose over any of them. Dull brown at the edges means it has been cut a while.
sources: USDA FSIS “The Color of Meat and Poultry”
USDA FSIS meat labeling and product dating guidance
University of Illinois Extension “Meat Shopping Safety Guidelines” https://extension.illinois.edu/meat-safety/shopping
Michigan State University Extension “The color of meat depends on myoglobin: Part 1” https://www.canr.msu.edu/news/the_color_of_meat_depends_on_myoglobin_part_1
Michigan State University Extension “Dates on meat packages” https://www.canr.msu.edu/news/dates_on_meat_packages_sell_by_use_by_freeze_by_packaged_on_expiration_date
entries.kristy_take: Color is oxygen, not quality. Check the seal, check for leaks, smell it. Those three beat the sticker.
buying_tips: Not slimy, and no off smell. Both, not either.
Fine marbling through the muscle beats a thick fat cap on the outside.
The package should be fully sealed, with no holes, tears or punctures, and not leaking meat juices.
Purple beef is vacuum-packed, not spoiled. Brown edges mean older, not unsafe.
Take it from the back of the case where it is coldest, and get it home cold.

labels_decoded.meaning: A store rotation instruction set by the retailer. Not a safety limit.
The liquid in the tray. What to check is the package: sealed, and not leaking it.

entries.tier_note: Color coming from oxygen is settled chemistry, which is why a sealed package and a smell test read more than the shade.
watch_out: Brownish or discolored meat is not automatically spoiled. Judge it by the seal and the smell, not the color alone.
A ‘packaged on’ date is not a safety cutoff. Fresh tray-wrapped meat generally holds up to three days refrigerated after packaging. A well-sealed vacuum pack can go up to seven.

entries.title: Dry-brining meat
entries.question: When should I salt meat, and is a brine worth it?
entries.decision: Salting a day ahead seasons the meat through and dries the surface.
entries.why: Salt pulls moisture out, then goes back in with it. The dried surface is what browns.
entries.short_answer: Salt early. A day ahead, salt draws out moisture that soaks back in, seasoning the meat through. It also helps the meat hold water as it cooks. Left uncovered in the fridge, the surface dries, and dry surfaces brown.
entries.detail: Salt early and skip the bucket. Applied a day ahead, salt dissolves in the meat’s own surface moisture, draws more out, and that concentrated brine is reabsorbed. That seasons the muscle through rather than sitting on it, and loosens the proteins so they hold on to water during cooking. Left uncovered in the fridge, the surface dries at the same time, and a dry surface is the whole precondition for browning. A wet brine does some of the same seasoning work and adds water while it does it, which is the problem: the extra moisture has to boil off before the surface can brown, so the crust arrives late or not at all. Dry-brining gets the interior seasoning without that trade. Timing scales with thickness. A large roast or a thick steak wants a day, chops and cuts under an inch are fine with an hour, and even fifteen minutes beats salting at the pan, because that is long enough for the salt to dissolve but not long enough to draw a wet film that then has to evaporate. The one place it inverts is ground meat. The amount is worth stating by weight rather than by spoon, because kosher salt brands differ by nearly half in density: a teaspoon of Morton is about 4.8 grams and a teaspoon of Diamond Crystal about 2.8, so the same spoon delivers wildly different salt.
entries.kristy_take: Salt the day before, uncovered. It is the cheapest thing you can do to a piece of meat.
sources: food-science work on salt diffusion and protein denaturation in muscle
Maillard browning and the surface-moisture threshold
published dry-brine ratios by cut (0.75–1.25% poultry, 1–1.5% beef steaks, 1.5–2% large roasts)
buying_tips: One percent of the meat by weight, about four and a half grams a pound.
A day ahead for a roast or a thick steak. An hour covers chops.
Uncovered, on a rack, so the surface can actually dry.
Without a scale: a rounded teaspoon and a half of Diamond Crystal per pound, or a level teaspoon of Morton.
A large roast or a brisket takes more, closer to one and a half percent.
watch_out: Kosher salt brands are not interchangeable by volume. A teaspoon of Morton weighs nearly twice a teaspoon of Diamond Crystal. At this ratio, that is the difference between seasoned and inedible.
Enhanced pork and koshered poultry arrive already salted. Read for ‘solution added’ and skip this on those.
Ground meat is the exception. Salt dissolves the proteins and the texture turns springy, so salt burgers as they hit the pan.
Skip the wet brine. It adds the water that then has to boil off before anything browns.
entries.tier_note: How salt moves through muscle, and why a dry surface browns and a wet one steams, are both basic food chemistry. The timing is the part people skip.

entries.title: What to ask the butcher
entries.question: What should I ask at the butcher counter?
entries.decision: The butcher knows what came in today and what needs selling.
entries.why: The counter is free expertise. Custom grinds, portioning and bones are usually included.
entries.short_answer: The service counter is free expertise most shoppers walk past. Ask what came in today and ask the sourcing question directly. Ask for a custom grind, a cut portioned your way, and bones and trim for stock.
entries.detail: A staffed counter answers things a package never will: whether the beef is grass-finished, whether the chicken was air-chilled, when it was actually cut. They will grind a chuck roast fresh, which beats the pre-packed tray and lets you choose the cut. They will french a rack, tie a roast, portion a whole fish. At most counters none of that costs extra. The cheap cuts sit in the same case, and the person behind the glass usually knows exactly how to cook them. Ask what is coming down in price this week, then build the week around the answer. Unsure of the cut, name the primal first: a roast from the chuck, a cut from the loin.
sources: USDA Institutional Meat Purchase Specifications (cut nomenclature)
MakeFoodSafe.com “Meat Grinding at Home Safety Tips” https://www.makefoodsafe.com/meat-grinding-at-home-safety-tips/
Rising Star Custom Meats “4 Questions You Should Always Ask Your Local Butchers” https://www.risingstarmeats.com/4-questions-you-should-always-ask-your-local-butchers
The Butcher’s Handbook “How to Order Meat Like a Pro: Butcher Counter Communication Guide” https://butchershandbook.com/guides/butcher-counter-terminology
entries.kristy_take: The counter is free expertise. Ask what came in today and what is cheap this week, then build dinner from the answer.
buying_tips: Ask what came in today, and what is coming down in price.
Ask for a custom grind. A chuck roast ground fresh beats the pre-packed tray.
Ask for bones and trim. Often cheap or free, and they make stock.
Ask the sourcing question outright: grass-finished, air-chilled, where from.
Ask them to portion it. Cutting, tying and boning are usually included.
entries.tier_note: Using the counter is a shopping habit offered as a standard, not a claim about the meat.
watch_out: ‘Aged’ covers two different things. Wet-aged beef rests in a vacuum bag and keeps its moisture. Dry-aged beef rests in open air, loses weight and comes out with a much more concentrated flavor. Ask which one it is.
Silverskin is connective tissue that does not break down in cooking. Ask to have it removed from a tenderloin or ribs.
Thickness is not fixed. Say how thick the steak should be, what size roast is needed and what lean-to-fat ratio the grind should have.
Unsure of the cut, name the section first: a roast from the chuck, a cut from the loin. That opens a real conversation about what is fresh.

entries.title: Chicken cuts: breast, thigh, whole bird
entries.question: Which cut of chicken should I buy?
entries.decision: Bone-in thighs carry more fat and collagen than breast meat.
entries.why: Dark meat is forgiving and hard to overcook. Boneless skinless is the priciest form of it.
entries.short_answer: Whole bird: cheapest per pound, and the carcass makes stock. Thighs carry more fat and flavor, and are hard to overcook. Breast is lean and dries fast. Bone-in, skin-on cuts cost less and cook better than boneless skinless.
entries.detail: Dark meat comes from muscles the bird actually used, so it carries more fat and stays juicy across a wide window of doneness. Breast is a low-use muscle: lean, quick, unforgiving. Bones conduct heat slowly and skin renders and bastes, which is why bone-in skin-on thighs are the most forgiving thing in the case. Boneless skinless breast is convenience paid for twice, once at the register and again in how fast it dries. A whole bird broken down at home gives you both kinds of meat plus a frame for broth, at the lowest cost per pound in the store. Thighs are dark meat: more fat, more flavor, and very hard to overcook. Breast is lean and fast and goes dry the moment you look away. Bone-in and skin-on cost less and cook better than boneless skinless, which is the most expensive way to buy the same bird.
sources: 9 CFR § 441.10 “Retained water in raw meat and poultry products” (Cornell LII) https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/9/441.10
entries.kristy_take: Bone-in thighs are the most forgiving protein in the store. A whole bird is the cheapest, and the frame makes stock.
buying_tips: Whole bird: cheapest per pound, and the carcass makes stock.
Thighs, bone-in and skin-on: forgiving, cheap, hard to overcook.
Breast: fast and lean. Pull it the moment it is done.
Boneless skinless is the priciest form of the same bird.
Check the label for ‘retained water’, and for ‘air-chilled’ if skin matters to you.

labels_decoded.meaning: Working muscle. More fat, more flavor, a wide margin for error.
Low-use muscle. Lean and fast, dries out quickly.

entries.tier_note: Skin rendering and basting is how the cut behaves; defaulting to skin-on thighs is the whole-food standard.

A raw single-ingredient bird may not carry retained water at all. The exception is when the processing that keeps it safe makes it unavoidable.

entries.title: Pork cuts and ‘solution added’ pork
entries.question: Which pork cut should I buy, and what does ‘solution added’ mean?
entries.decision: Pork shoulder is the forgiving cut; enhanced pork is pumped with saltwater.
entries.why: Shoulder is the value cut in the case. ‘Enhanced’ means injected brine, sold by the pound.
entries.short_answer: Hard-working muscles go low and slow, lean ones go fast. Shoulder is the cheap braising and pulled-pork cut. Loin and tenderloin are lean and quick. ‘Contains up to X% solution’ means injected saltwater, sold by the pound and already salted.
entries.detail: Same rule as beef: hard-working muscles go low and slow, lean ones go fast. The figure to find is ‘contains up to X% solution’, which means injected saltwater and phosphates. A large share of retail pork is pumped with a solution of water, salt and phosphates to hold moisture, because modern pork is bred lean and dries out. The percentage has to be declared. It is not unsafe, and it does make a lean chop more forgiving, but it changes what you paid for and it pre-seasons the meat, so a second brine oversalts it. Unenhanced pork browns better and tastes more like pork. Shoulder is the value cut of the whole animal: fatty, forgiving, and it feeds a crowd for very little.
sources: USDA FSIS labeling requirements for enhanced and solution-added meat
USDA Institutional Meat Purchase Specifications (pork cut nomenclature)
9 CFR § 317.2 labeling of raw meat and poultry containing added solutions (Cornell LII) https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/9/317.2
entries.kristy_take: Pork shoulder is the best value in the meat case. And read the fine print: ‘up to 12% solution’ is water sold by the pound.
buying_tips: Braise or pull: shoulder, Boston butt, picnic, country-style ribs.
Fast and lean: loin chops, tenderloin. Pull them early.
Read for ‘contains up to X% solution’. That is injected brine.
Enhanced pork is already salted. Skip your own brine, and expect less browning.
Hormones are banned in pork production, so ‘no added hormones’ on pork is a freebie.

labels_decoded.term: Enhanced / contains up to X% solution
labels_decoded.meaning: Injected with saltwater and phosphates. Declared by law, and sold by weight.

entries.title: ‘Uncured’ deli meat
entries.question: Is ‘uncured’ deli meat actually nitrite-free?
entries.decision: ‘Uncured’ meat is cured, using celery powder instead of added nitrite.
entries.why: Celery juice powder is a concentrated natural nitrate source. Same chemistry, different source.
entries.short_answer: No. ‘Uncured’ packages must carry a qualifier, along the lines of ‘except those naturally occurring in celery powder’. Celery juice powder is a concentrated natural nitrate source. So the meat is cured, with a vegetable-derived agent, not a synthetic one.
entries.detail: No, and the package says so if you find the asterisk. ‘Uncured, no nitrates or nitrites added’ is required to be followed by a qualifier along the lines of ‘except those naturally occurring in celery powder’. USDA labeling rules force that qualifier, which is why every ‘uncured’ package carries a footnote most shoppers never read. The chemistry that fixes the color and preserves the meat is the same either way; only the source of the nitrate differs, and measured residual levels are broadly comparable. That does not make it a scam, it makes it a sourcing preference, and it is worth knowing that ‘uncured’ is a different statement from ‘no nitrites’. The bigger question at the deli case is how much processed meat a week holds, not which curing agent was used.
sources: USDA FSIS labeling policy on ‘uncured’ and ‘no nitrate or nitrite added’ claims
Peer-reviewed comparisons of residual nitrite in conventionally and naturally cured meats
Niche Meat Processor Assistance Network “Uncured Bacon” https://www.nichemeatprocessing.org/uncured-bacon/
9 CFR § 317.17 curing-agent declaration and “uncured” labeling (Cornell LII) https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/9/317.17
entries.kristy_take: ‘Uncured’ means cured with celery powder. The asterisk on the package says so. Same chemistry, different source.
buying_tips: Find the asterisk. ‘Uncured’ is always qualified on the label.
Celery powder is a natural nitrate source. It is a curing agent, not the absence of one.

entries.title: Mercury by fish
aliases: which fish are low in mercury
entries.question: Which fish are low in mercury and which are high?
entries.decision: Sardines, salmon and skipjack are small fish that live short lives.
entries.why: Mercury tracks size and lifespan. The big long-lived predators carry the most.
entries.short_answer: It tracks size and lifespan almost perfectly. Small, short-lived fish carry the least. Big long-lived predators carry the most. Sardines, salmon and canned light tuna sit at the bottom. Swordfish, shark, king mackerel and bigeye tuna sit at the top.
entries.detail: Methylmercury accumulates up the food chain, so a fish that ate thousands of smaller fish across twenty years carries far more than one that lived two years on plankton. That is why the pattern is so predictable by species. FDA and EPA publish it as a three-tier list (Best Choices, Good Choices, Choices to Avoid) and direct the advice at pregnant and nursing women and young children. This is information about the fish. Anything about a personal medical situation belongs with a doctor. Canned light tuna is usually skipjack.

entries.kristy_take: Small and short-lived is the entire rule. Sardines, salmon and skipjack sit at the bottom of the chain, and a tin of any of them costs less than a fillet.
buying_tips: Lowest: sardines, anchovies, salmon, shrimp, scallops, tilapia, cod, pollock, catfish, canned light tuna.
Middle: albacore and yellowfin tuna, halibut, grouper, snapper, mahi mahi.
Highest: swordfish, shark, king mackerel, marlin, orange roughy, bigeye tuna, Gulf tilefish.
‘Light’ tuna is usually skipjack and sits well below ‘white’ albacore.
FDA and EPA aim the advice at pregnant and nursing women and young children. Anything medical is a doctor’s call.
Sardines and canned salmon, bones left in, are shelf-stable and low on the chain. Canned is the cheapest way to eat either one.

A larger tuna. Higher than light.

entries.title: Telling fresh at the fish counter
aliases: how to tell fish is fresh
entries.question: How do I tell if fish at the counter is fresh?
entries.decision: Fresh fish smells of clean seawater, or of nothing at all.
entries.why: Sharp or ammonia means it has gone. Then check the eyes, the gills and the ice.
entries.short_answer: Smell first. Fresh fish smells like clean seawater or like almost nothing. Sharp fishy or ammonia means it has gone. Whole fish: clear domed eyes, bright red gills, flesh that springs back. Fillets: a translucent sheen, no pooled liquid.
entries.detail: The ‘fishy’ smell people associate with fish is the smell of it breaking down, which makes it the single best gauge in the case. Whole fish tell you more than fillets, because eyes, gills and skin all age visibly. On a fillet the tell is gaping: muscle segments separate as it ages and the flesh loses its sheen. Ice matters as much as the fish, so it should be sitting on plenty of it and not in a puddle. Asking them to hand you a piece to smell is completely normal, and any good counter will. On a whole fish the scales should be tight. On a fillet the flakes should still hold together, with no browning at the edges and no liquid pooled underneath.
sources: FDA Fish and Fishery Products Hazards and Controls Guidance (sensory evaluation)
Nofima “How to check how fresh fish is” https://nofima.com/worth-knowing/how-to-check-how-fresh-fish-is/ (gills as the single best freshness check; eye and skin sheen; the date alone is not reliable)
entries.kristy_take: Ask to smell it. Clean seawater or nothing means yes. Sharp and fishy means put it back.
buying_tips: Smell it. Clean and briny is right. Sharp, fishy or ammonia is not.
Whole fish: clear domed eyes, bright red gills, tight scales, flesh that springs back.
Fillets: a translucent sheen, flakes holding together, no browning at the edge.
It should sit on plenty of ice, not in a pool of its own liquid.
Ask when it came in and whether it was previously frozen. Both are fair questions.

labels_decoded.meaning: Flakes separating on a fillet. A sign it has aged.

entries.tier_note: The smell it gives off and the ice it is bedded in are both documented freshness checks, not opinions about the fish.
watch_out: If only one check is possible, make it the gills. Red means recently slaughtered; brown, gray or green means the fish is past fresh.
The date on the label is not the whole story. Breakdown starts at slaughter and runs faster or slower with handling and storage. A fish inside its date can still show gray, matte, sunken eyes.

entries.title: Buying canned fish
entries.question: What should I look for in canned fish?
entries.decision: Tinned fish in olive oil or water, bones and skin left in.
entries.why: The list should read fish, oil or water, salt. Anything longer is a sauce.
entries.short_answer: Read what it is packed in. Olive oil or water are the clean options. Plenty of tins use soybean, cottonseed or unnamed ‘vegetable oil’. Buy sardines and salmon with the bones and skin left in.
entries.detail: Canned fish is one of the best value whole foods in the store, and the differences between tins are almost entirely the pack medium and what else went in. Oil-packed carries more flavor and, in good olive oil, is worth using in the dish rather than pouring away. Water-packed is leaner and neutral. ‘Vegetable oil’ on a tin is nearly always a seed oil blend and the label will not name which. Skin-on, bone-in sardines and salmon keep the whole small fish intact, which is much of why the tin is worth buying. Flavored tins in sauces bring added sugar and a long list, so read those like any packaged food. Soybean, cottonseed or unnamed ‘vegetable oil’ matters if seed oils are a line you hold. The ingredient list should read fish, oil or water, and salt; anything longer is a sauce.

entries.title: Which farmed fish are worth buying
entries.question: Is farmed fish worth buying?
entries.decision: Farmed trout, char and shellfish are worth buying without hesitation.
entries.why: ‘Farmed’ is not a verdict. Mussels and oysters feed themselves by filtering water.
entries.short_answer: It depends entirely on the species and the operation, never on the word ‘farmed’. Farmed mussels, oysters and clams are the standout: they filter water and need no feed. Farmed trout, arctic char and barramundi are generally well regarded.
entries.detail: Aquaculture is not one thing. A rope of mussels hanging in a bay takes nothing and adds nothing. A closed recirculating tank system for trout or char is tightly controlled. An open net pen or a coastal shrimp pond depends on the standards of the country and the company running it. So the useful question at the counter is which species and where from, rather than farmed or wild. Wild is the whole-food-standard preference where it is affordable, and that is a preference, not a health verdict on farmed fish. Eating the fish beats skipping it. Farmed shellfish feed themselves by filtering water and need no feed at all. Salmon and shrimp vary enormously by producer and country, which is where certification and origin do real work.

entries.title: Seafood seals: MSC, ASC, BAP
entries.question: Do the sustainability seals on seafood mean anything?
entries.decision: MSC is the wild-catch seal worth trusting; farm seals set a minimum.
entries.why: Each seal answers one narrow question, and none of them speaks to freshness.
entries.short_answer: The blue MSC label covers wild fisheries and how the stock is managed. ASC and BAP audit farms and set a floor, not a recommendation. Seafood Watch is not a label at all, it is a ratings guide.
entries.detail: Each seal answers one question. MSC audits whether a wild fishery is managed so the stock holds and the gear does not wreck the habitat. ASC and BAP audit farms. BAP’s stars count the audited links: one is the processing plant, four adds the farm, hatchery and feed mill. All three publish their standards and send auditors, which is more than an unbacked word on a package offers. What none of them tell you is anything about the fish in front of you: how fresh it is, how it tastes, or how it was handled since. MSC is the seal that lines up with buying wild in the first place. ASC and BAP rest on published standards and real auditors. BAP’s one-to-four stars count how far up the chain the audit reached. Seafood Watch is a ratings guide you look up.

entries.title: How to pick it, item by item
entries.question: How do I tell if this particular fruit or vegetable is any good?
entries.decision: The heavier piece of two the same size holds more juice.
entries.why: Weight means water content, not pith. One habit that beats every color rule going.
entries.short_answer: Each item has one or two checks that work, almost never color. Heavy for its size is the near-universal one. Smell the stem end on anything that ripens off the plant. Turn berry containers over, where mold starts.
entries.detail: Fruit that keeps ripening after picking (melon, peach, avocado, banana, mango, pear) gives you smell and give as signals. Fruit that does not ripen further once picked (berries, citrus, grapes, pineapple, cherries) has to be bought ready, so those checks are about weight and damage instead. Vegetables are mostly a firmness question: a limp stalk or a rubbery skin means it has been out of the ground a while and lost water. The single best habit is picking up two of the same thing and comparing them by weight. The heavier one is almost always better.
sources: University extension produce selection and ripening guidance

University of Georgia Extension “How to Pick a Ripe Watermelon” https://site.extension.uga.edu/evansag/2026/06/how-to-pick-a-ripe-watermelon/
entries.kristy_take: Pick up two and take the heavier one. That one habit beats every color rule going.
buying_tips: Cantaloupe: creamy gold under the netting, a sweet smell at the stem end, slight give.
Watermelon: a deep yellow field spot, heavy for its size, a hollow thunk.
Pineapple: sweet at the base, deep green leaves, a slight give in the shell. Color is not the tell.
Tomatoes: fragrant at the stem, heavy for their size, and never from the cold case.
Stone fruit: fragrant, with a slight give at the shoulder rather than the tip.
Citrus: heavy for its size, with thin smooth skin. Weight beats color.
Asparagus: tight closed tips and a cut end that is not dried and split.
Broccoli and cauliflower: tight dense heads, no yellowing between the florets.
Leafy greens: perky rather than limp, with no slimy dark patches at the stem base.
Avocado: pop the stem nub. Green under it means ripe, brown means overripe, and stuck fast means give it days.
Press with your palm, never your fingertips. Fingertip pressure is what bruises the bin.
Buy at staggered firmness so they ripen across the week rather than all on Tuesday.
watch_out: Watermelon: a pale green or white ground spot means likely underripe. Creamy yellow is the one to take.
A shiny watermelon rind tends to be underripe. Dull skin is the good sign, not the bad one.
The thump: ripe sounds dull and hollow, unripe sounds high-pitched or metallic.
pick_steps: Pick up two the same size and take the heavier one.
Press with your palm, never fingertips, and buy at staggered firmness.
Watermelon: creamy yellow ground spot, dull rind, a dull hollow thump.

Citrus should feel heavy with thin, smooth skin; color is not the tell. Vegetables are a firmness check: tight asparagus tips, dense broccoli heads without yellowing, perky greens without slime. entries.title: Picking berries
entries.question: How do I pick a good carton of berries?
entries.decision: One soft berry underneath turns the whole carton within a day.
entries.why: Berries mold from the bottom up under their own weight, long before the top layer shows it.
entries.short_answer: Turn the container over first. The bottom fruit carries the load, so it bruises and molds first. A dry, clean underside means it was packed recently and has not sat wet. Juice or a fuzzy spot means decay is running.
entries.detail: Berries do not ripen after picking. Unlike a peach or a cantaloupe, what is in the carton is exactly what you are buying. There is no counter-ripening to rescue an underripe punnet, and no reason to buy firm and wait. That makes the carton itself the whole decision. Weight and moisture are what work against it: the bottom layer carries the load, condensation inside a clamshell keeps that layer damp, and mold spreads berry to berry by contact. Clamshells also get re-stacked at the store, so a fresh-looking top layer can sit on fruit that arrived days earlier. Buy them cold, keep them dry, and wash them at the moment you eat them rather than when you unpack. The top layer stays presentable long after the carton has turned, and one furry berry takes the punnet.

Ohio State University Extension “Selecting, Storing, and Serving Ohio Berries” (HYG-5531) https://ohioline.osu.edu/factsheet/HYG-5531

buying_tips: A dry, unstained bottom on the carton. That is the whole check.
No fuzzy white or gray spot on any berry. One takes the punnet.
Green caps still fresh on strawberries, not browned and dry.
Deep, even color for the variety, and uniform size in the container.
Buy them cold, from the refrigerated display rather than a room-temperature stack.

entries.title: Making produce last the week
entries.question: How do I keep produce from going off before I use it?
entries.decision: Washing produce before storing it traps moisture and speeds rot.
entries.why: Moisture is what rots a drawer. Keep the ripening-gas fruit away from greens and berries.
entries.short_answer: Three rules cover most of it. Keep ripening-gas fruit away from greens and berries. Do not wash anything until you use it. Keep a short list out of the fridge: tomatoes, potatoes, onions, garlic, whole melon, unripe stone fruit.
entries.detail: Apples, bananas, avocados, tomatoes and stone fruit give off the ripening gas, and greens, broccoli, cucumbers and berries are ethylene sensitive and wilt fast beside it. Ethylene is a plant hormone that triggers ripening and it works on neighbors, which is why a bowl of apples ages the lettuce next to it. Moisture is the other half: water sitting on a leaf or a berry is where mold starts, so the rinse belongs at the moment of eating rather than at unpacking. Cold wrecks texture and flavor in a few specific things. Tomatoes go mealy below about 55F, potatoes convert starch to sugar and brown oddly when cooked, and onions and garlic soften and sprout. Herbs and asparagus keep best standing in a little water like cut flowers, and greens keep best dry with a towel in the bag.
sources: USDA and university extension postharvest storage guidance
FDA produce storage and safety guidance

Michigan State University Extension “All fruit and vegetables are not created equal when it comes to proper storage conditions” https://www.canr.msu.edu/news/all-fruit-and-vegetables-are-not-created-equal-when-it-comes-to-proper-storage-conditions

University of Massachusetts Amherst Extension “Optimal Storage Conditions and Ethylene Sensitivity of Fall Storage Crops” https://www.umass.edu/agriculture-food-environment/vegetable/fact-sheets/optimal-storage-conditions-ethylene-sensitivity-of-fall-storage-crops
entries.kristy_take: Wash it when you eat it, not when you unpack it. Half of what rots in a fridge was rinsed on the way in.
buying_tips: Separate the gas producers (apples, bananas, avocados, tomatoes, stone fruit) from greens and berries.
Do not wash anything until you are about to use it.
Never refrigerate: tomatoes, potatoes, onions, garlic, whole melon, unripe stone fruit.
Herbs and asparagus: stand them in a little water, loosely covered.
Greens: dry, with a paper towel in the bag to take up moisture.
Buy at staggered ripeness so the whole week does not turn on Tuesday.
entries.tier_note: Ethylene ripening its neighbors, and moisture rotting a drawer, are both well established.
watch_out: Ethylene-sensitive vegetables stored near producers spoil faster. Cabbage and Brussels sprouts yellow or crack, carrots turn bitter, cucumbers break down sooner.
Apples, pears, peaches, plums, cantaloupe and tomatoes give off significant ethylene. Keep them off the counter with anything sensitive.
pick_steps: Keep apples, bananas, avocados, tomatoes and stone fruit apart from greens and berries.
Wash nothing until use; store greens dry with a paper towel.
Leave tomatoes, potatoes, onions, garlic, whole melon and unripe stone fruit unrefrigerated.
entries.science: Apples, pears, stone fruit, cantaloupe and tomatoes give off ethylene, a ripening gas that ages neighbors. Near producers, cabbage and Brussels sprouts yellow or crack, carrots turn bitter, and cucumbers break down sooner. Water on a leaf or berry is where mold starts. entries.title: Reviving wilted greens
entries.question: Can I bring limp greens back, or are they finished?
entries.decision: Limp greens have lost water, not gone bad, and they come back.
entries.why: The cells have gone slack. Given cold water they refill and the leaf goes rigid again.
entries.short_answer: Most limp greens are thirsty, not spoiled. Water pressure in the cells holds a leaf rigid. When it drops, the leaf goes limp, but intact cells take the water back. Thirty minutes in cold water restores most of it.
entries.detail: The same mechanism explains why the trick is worth doing on more than lettuce. Celery, carrots, radishes, chard, kale and soft herbs all go limp by the same route and all firm up again. Cutting a sliver off the stem end first matters for anything with a stem, because the vessels seal and a fresh cut lets water move again, exactly as it does for cut flowers. Cold matters too. Cold water is taken up more readily and it firms the cell walls at the same time. Bagged, pre-washed greens revive least, because they have already been cut and a cut edge does not reseal. What does not come back is anything that has actually started to break down.
entries.kristy_take: Cold water and half an hour. Most of the greens in the bin did not need to be there.
sources: plant physiology of turgor pressure and cell-wall rigidity
postharvest handling guidance on rehydrating leafy vegetables
buying_tips: Thirty minutes in cold water covers most of it. An hour for the worst of them.
Cut a sliver off the stem end first, the way you would for cut flowers.
Spin or pat them dry afterward, or the water you just added rots them in the drawer.
watch_out: Yellowing, sliminess or a smell is decay, and cold water does nothing for it. That one goes out.
Pre-washed bagged greens revive least. They were cut before you bought them and a cut edge does not reseal.
pick_steps: Cut a sliver off the stem end, like cut flowers.
Soak thirty minutes in cold water, an hour for the worst.
Spin or pat them dry before they go back in the drawer.
entries.science: Limp greens are mostly thirsty, not spoiled. Water pressure in the cells holds a leaf rigid, and intact cells take water back. A fresh cut reopens sealed stem vessels, and cold water is taken up more readily. Pre-washed bagged greens revive least, because a cut edge does not reseal. Yellowing, sliminess or a smell is decay, and cold water does nothing for it.
entries.tier_note: Turgor pressure is basic plant physiology, and it is why a leaf goes rigid again. Nothing about it makes an old leaf new.

entries.title: Pasteurized, ultra-pasteurized, homogenized
aliases: why does organic milk last so long
entries.question: What is the difference between pasteurized, ultra-pasteurized and homogenized milk?
entries.decision: Plain pasteurized goes through one heat step; ultra goes far hotter.
entries.why: Fewer steps is the whole-food standard. Ultra buys months on a date and costs the milk its character.
entries.short_answer: Fewer steps is the standard. Pasteurization is a short heat step. Ultra-pasteurization runs far hotter, which puts a date months out and stops the milk culturing. Homogenization is not heat. It breaks the fat small so the cream never rises.
entries.detail: Pasteurization runs around 161F for fifteen seconds. Ultra-pasteurization goes to roughly 280F, which is what puts a date months out on a carton and what makes the milk refuse to culture. Homogenization forces the fat into droplets small enough that cream never rises. These three get muddled constantly. Heat is about shelf life and safety; homogenization is about texture and whether the cream separates. Ultra-pasteurization changes flavor noticeably and makes milk reluctant to culture into yogurt or cheese, which is the practical reason people avoid it rather than a nutritional one. On the whole-food standard the read is simple: fewer processing steps, so plain pasteurized and non-homogenized where the store carries them. That is a preference about processing, not a claim that ultra-pasteurized milk is bad for anyone.
sources: FDA Pasteurized Milk Ordinance (time and temperature standards)
FDA milk labeling and processing definitions

Michigan State University Extension, dairy processing article https://www.canr.msu.edu/news/they_did_what_to_your_milk (homogenization forces milk at high pressure through small holes so fat does not rise; no health benefits or risks associated with it; non-homogenized milk available from some bottlers)
entries.kristy_take: The shortest date on the shelf is usually the least-handled milk.
buying_tips: ‘Ultra-pasteurized’ or ‘UHT’ on the carton explains a date months out.
Ultra-pasteurized milk resists culturing. Skip it for homemade yogurt.

entries.title: Live cultures, kefir and skyr
entries.question: How do I know the cultures are still alive?
entries.decision: Heat treatment after fermenting kills the bacteria it just grew.
entries.why: Heat treatment after culturing ends the ferment. Strained styles hold more protein per spoon.
entries.short_answer: A tub can be yogurt and carry nothing living. What makes one shelf-stable is exactly what ends it. The cold case is the first filter, the seal the second. Strained Greek and skyr are thicker, with more protein per spoon.
entries.detail: Yogurt is milk plus two required cultures, and everything past that (extra strains, straining, thickeners) is what separates one tub from another. ‘Live and Active Cultures’ is a seal with a defined threshold behind it, and heat-treated shelf-stable yogurts do not carry it, which is the cleanest tell on the shelf. Straining pours off whey and concentrates the protein, which is why a cup of Greek reads so differently from a cup of regular. Kefir ferments with a broader mix of bacteria and yeasts than yogurt does. None of this is a question about sugar; that is the plain-versus-flavored call and it is a separate card. Kefir is a drinkable ferment with a wider mix of cultures than yogurt.

entries.title: Cream, half-and-half, and ‘creamer’
entries.question: What is the difference between cream and coffee creamer?
entries.decision: Non-dairy creamer is oil, sugar and thickeners, with no milk.
entries.why: Cream has a legal fat minimum. Creamer is oil, sweetener and emulsifiers built to imitate it.
entries.short_answer: Cream is dairy with a legal fat minimum. ‘Non-dairy creamer’ is not dairy at all. It is typically water or corn syrup solids, an oil, and emulsifiers, flavors and thickeners built to imitate cream. Compare the two lists.
entries.detail: Heavy cream is at least 36% milkfat, light whipping 30 to 36, half-and-half 10.5 to 18. Standards of identity fix what cream can mean, which is why those fat percentages are consistent across every carton. Creamer has no such standard because it is a formulated product. The oil in it is usually a refined seed oil, and the sweetness usually comes from corn syrup solids or sugar, with the flavored versions adding more of both. Some cartons of real cream carry stabilizers like carrageenan or gellan gum, so a short list is worth checking on the dairy side too. Whole milk, half-and-half or real cream all do the job with a list you can read out loud. Read the two ingredient lists side by side and it takes three seconds.
sources: FDA standards of identity for cream products, 21 CFR 131

entries.title: Flour: bleached, enriched, whole
entries.question: Which flour should I buy, and what does ‘enriched’ mean?
entries.decision: Unbleached flour skips the chemical whitening step bleached flour goes through.
entries.why: Protein content picks the flour. Whole wheat keeps the germ, and that oil turns.
entries.short_answer: Protein content picks the flour. Bread flour is highest and builds chew. All-purpose is the middle. Cake and pastry flour are lowest and stay tender. Whole wheat keeps the bran and germ, so it turns rancid far sooner.
entries.detail: Refining strips the bran and germ and leaves the starchy endosperm, which is what makes white flour pale and shelf-stable. Enrichment is a regulated add-back of thiamin, riboflavin, niacin, folic acid and iron, and it is standard on most white flour sold in the US. Bleaching speeds up the same softening that months of air exposure would have done. Whole wheat still carries the oil in the germ, so it keeps for months rather than years and belongs in the freezer if it is not going quickly. Its bran also cuts gluten strands, which is why an all-whole-wheat loaf comes out denser. ‘Enriched’ means B vitamins and iron were added back after refining removed them. ‘Bleached’ means treated with a chemical whitening agent, while ‘unbleached’ was simply aged with air. Whole wheat behaves differently in baking.
sources: FDA standards of identity for enriched flour, 21 CFR 137
FDA regulations on flour bleaching and maturing agents

entries.kristy_take: Unbleached over bleached, and keep whole wheat in the freezer. The germ is still in it, and that oil turns.
watch_out: Whole wheat flour keeps the germ and its oil, and heat, air and moisture are what turn it. In a pantry at room temperature, a month is the outside window. Seal air out, or other flavors and odors move in.
buying_tips: Bread flour for chew, all-purpose for most things, pastry flour for tender.
‘Enriched’ means vitamins and iron added back after refining. Standard on white flour.
‘Unbleached’ was aged with air. ‘Bleached’ was chemically whitened.
Whole wheat carries the oil in the germ. Buy small and keep it in the freezer.

Treated with a whitening and maturing agent.

entries.title: Buying from the bulk bins
entries.question: Is the bulk bin section actually a good deal?
entries.decision: Dry staples keep well in bulk; anything oily turns rancid first.
entries.why: Turnover is everything. Oil goes rancid in a slow bin, whatever the price says.
entries.short_answer: Yes, when the bin turns over. Grains, beans, lentils, oats, rice and spices are dramatically cheaper by weight. Nuts, seeds and whole-grain flours carry oil that goes rancid. Pick a full, busy bin and smell what you scoop.
entries.detail: Bulk pricing strips out the packaging and the brand, which is most of what a shelf-stable staple costs. Spices are the extreme case, where a scoop from a bin costs a fraction of the same weight in a jar and is usually fresher because the bin moves. The risk sits entirely with the fatty items. Rancidity is the real quality question in this aisle, and it announces itself: rancid nuts and seeds smell like old paint or crayons and taste sharp and bitter. Bring your own jars where the store allows it, and note the tare weight. Spices especially are cheaper by weight, and you buy exactly what you need. The catch is turnover: nuts, seeds and whole-grain flours carry oil that goes rancid, so a slow bin is a bad buy at any price.
sources: FDA retail bulk food handling guidance

Civil Eats “Is Shopping in Bulk Still a Sustainable Choice?” https://civileats.com/2023/08/22/is-shopping-in-bulk-still-a-sustainable-choice/ (a chain insisted the FDA food code forbids refilling your own container in the bulk aisle; the FDA describes the food code as a model offered for adoption by state and local governments, so the rule is the store’s)

The Counter, bulk-bin hygiene reporting https://thecounter.org/bulk-bins-grocery-stores-bring-your-own-container-covid-19/ (the real touchpoint is customers’ repeated touching of the same equipment, gravity bin and scoop bin handles and scales, rather than the container a shopper brings)
entries.kristy_take: Bulk is unbeatable on grains, beans and spices. On nuts and whole-grain flour it depends entirely on how fast that bin moves.
buying_tips: Best value: rice, oats, beans, lentils, dried fruit and especially spices.
Riskiest: nuts, seeds and whole-grain flours. Oil goes rancid in a slow bin.
Full busy bins turn over. A dusty half-empty one does not.
Smell it before it goes in the cart. Rancid reads as paint, crayon or bitter.
Buy what you will use in a month, and store it airtight and dark.
watch_out: The scoop, the bin handle and the scale are touched by every shopper before you. The container you bring is not the exposed part.
Bring-your-own-container rules vary by store. The FDA food code is a model offered to states and cities. A store citing it is stating its own policy, not a single national rule.
entries.tier_note: Rancidity in a slow bin is real. Which bins to trust is a shopping standard, not a rule.

entries.title: Whole spices and toasting
entries.question: Are whole spices worth the trouble over ground?
entries.decision: Ground spice loses its oils within months; whole spice keeps them.
entries.why: The aroma is volatile oil. Grinding opens the surface up and it leaves from there.
entries.short_answer: A spice’s flavor is its oil, and that oil escapes into the air. Whole, it stays sealed inside the seed or bark for a couple of years. Ground, it is gone within months. Grind as you go.
entries.detail: Toasting is worth separating from grinding. A dry pan over medium heat until the smell arrives across the kitchen does two things: it drives volatile compounds to the surface and it starts browning reactions in the seed that build flavors that were not there before. Toast whole, then grind, and use it — toasted spice fades faster than raw whole spice, so it is not something to do in a batch and store. A blade grinder is adequate and a mortar is better for anything you want texture from. A handful of spices are only sold ground because the whole form is impractical to break down at home, and those are worth buying in the smallest quantity you will actually finish. What you are buying in a spice is volatile oil. Ground, the surface area jumps and the same oil is off into the air within months, which is why a jar of ground cumin that smells of nothing is not spoiled, it is just empty. Warming them first drives the oils out where you can taste them.
entries.kristy_take: Whole, and grind what you need. A jar of ground spice is a jar with a clock on it.
sources: volatile-compound retention studies on whole versus ground spice storage
food-science references on dry-roasting and aromatic release

Aradwad et al. “Key issues and challenges in spice grinding,” Cleaner Engineering and Technology Vol. 5, Dec 2021 https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666790821001654 (heat-induced quality loss is a primary technical challenge in spice grinding; grinding needs special emphasis considering significant quality loss due to heat generation)
buying_tips: Whole spices hold for a couple of years. Ground ones are tired inside six months.
A dry pan over medium heat, until you can smell them across the kitchen.
Buy from a bin that turns over, in the smallest amount you will finish.
watch_out: Grinding itself makes heat. Heat during grinding is a primary way a spice loses quality before it is even in the jar. Small batches, ground as you go.
Toasted spice fades faster than whole. Toast what you are about to use, not a batch for the cupboard.
entries.tier_note: Volatile oils leaving faster once ground is straightforward chemistry, and toasting before the grind follows from it.

entries.title: Telling when fats have turned
aliases: how to tell if oil is rancid
entries.question: How do I tell if nuts, oil or flour have gone rancid?
entries.decision: Oils and nuts go rancid quietly, with no mold to warn you.
entries.why: Oxidized oil has a smell nothing else has. No date on the package will tell you.
entries.short_answer: Nuts, whole-grain flour and oils all carry fat that goes off. The tell is a smell like old paint, crayons, putty, or a dusty cupboard. The printed date does not predict it. Heat, light and air set the clock.
entries.detail: Oxidation is fat reacting with air, and light, heat and time all speed it up. That is the whole reason good olive oil comes in dark glass and gets stored away from the stove, and why whole-grain flour keeps months while white flour keeps almost indefinitely. The peppery catch at the back of the throat in fresh olive oil is a different sensation from the flat bitter scratch of a rancid one, and the difference is learnable in a single side-by-side taste. Once you can smell it, the bulk bin, the back of the pantry and the half-used oil bottle all become easy calls. The tell is a smell most people already know without a name for it. Nothing on the label predicts it, because the clock starts at pressing or milling and runs on heat, light and air rather than on the printed date.
sources: Peer-reviewed literature on lipid oxidation in foods
UC Davis Olive Center sensory standards for olive oil defects

America’s Test Kitchen “How to Tell If Olive Oil Is Rancid” https://www.americastestkitchen.com/articles/1224-how-to-tell-if-olive-oil-is-rancid (heat, air, light, and time will wreck the best olive oil; rancid oil has a distinctive smell like varnish, putty, old walnuts, or crayons, and rancidity is more obvious in the mouth, so take a tiny sip when in doubt; store cool, dark, tightly capped, and use it up promptly)
entries.kristy_take: Old paint and crayons is the smell. Once you know it, half the back of the pantry starts making sense.
buying_tips: Buy oil in a dark bottle, in a size you will finish inside two months.
Keep whole-grain flour and shelled nuts in the freezer. The germ oil is what turns.
Smell a bulk bin before you fill a bag from it.
watch_out: Rancid oil smells like varnish, putty, old walnuts or crayons. Rancidity is more obvious in the mouth than in the nose. A tiny sip settles a smell you are unsure of.
Heat, air, light and time are what turn it. A cool dark place, tightly capped, and use it up promptly.
entries.tier_note: The paint-and-crayon smell is oxidized fat, a quality problem rather than a safety one, and it is flagged on exactly that basis.

has my olive oil gone bad
what does rancid smell like

entries.title: Buying real extra-virgin olive oil
entries.question: How do I buy real extra-virgin olive oil, and what do the grades mean?
entries.decision: Extra virgin means cold-pressed, and a harvest date tells you how fresh.
entries.why: Olive oil is widely adulterated. ‘Pure’, ‘classic’ and ‘light’ all mean refined oil.
entries.short_answer: Extra virgin uses no heat or solvent, and has to pass lab and taste tests. ‘Pure’, ‘classic’ and ‘light’ are refined oil with some virgin added. Look for a recent harvest date, a dark bottle and one country of origin.
entries.detail: Grade and provenance are two separate checks and a bottle has to pass both. On grade: pomace oil is solvent-extracted from the paste left after pressing and is a different product; ‘first cold pressed’ is a legacy phrase with no added legal force. On provenance: ‘packed in [country]’ names where it was bottled, not where the olives grew, and ‘product of’ is the phrase that names the origin. A harvest date beats a best-by date every time, because the oil degrades from the day it is pressed. Dark glass or tin protects it from light, and a price that is unusually low for extra-virgin is a flag rather than a find. Extra virgin is mechanically extracted with no heat or solvent and has to pass both a chemical limit and a taste panel. Virgin is the same process with a looser limit. ‘Light’ refers to color and taste rather than calories. Past the grade, olive oil is one of the more adulterated products in the store.
sources: International Olive Council trade standard for olive oils
USDA AMS United States Standards for Grades of Olive Oil (voluntary)
FDA labeling rules on country of origin

UC Davis News “Study finds most imported olive oil fails international standards” https://www.ucdavis.edu/food/news/study-finds-most-imported-olive-oil-fails-international-standards (69 percent of imported oils sampled, against 10 percent of California oils, failed internationally accepted standards for extra virgin; the failed oils had defects such as rancidity)

UC Davis Olive Center “Study finds widespread quality problems in imported extra-virgin olive oil” https://olivecenter.ucdavis.edu/news-events/news/study-finds-widespread-quality-problems-imported-extra-virgin-olive-oil (73 percent of samples from the five top-selling imported brands failed two IOC-accredited taste panels; quality oils show the most recent harvest year and come in containers that keep out light)
entries.kristy_take: Harvest date, dark bottle, one country. Everything else on the front is decoration.
entries.instead: Butter or ghee for anything cooked. Whole-food fats, with no harvest date to check.
buying_tips: Extra virgin: mechanically extracted, no heat or solvent, taste-panel tested.
Look for a HARVEST date, not just ‘best by’. Buy recent.
Dark glass or tin protects it from light; store away from the stove.
Single country of origin, named with ‘product of’.
‘First cold pressed’ is a legacy phrase and adds nothing legally.

labels_decoded.meaning: Mechanically extracted, within a strict acidity limit, and taste-panel tested.
The same extraction with a looser limit.
Refined oil with a little virgin blended back. ‘Light’ means color and flavor.
Solvent-extracted from the paste left after pressing.
Where it was bottled. Not where the olives grew.

entries.tier_note: The grades are legal definitions with a taste panel behind them, and the origin wording is regulated. Both are readable off the bottle.
watch_out: ‘Pure’, ‘classic’ and ‘light’ all mean refined oil. ‘Light’ refers to flavor and color, not calories.
Pomace oil is solvent-extracted from the paste left after pressing. A different product.
‘Packed in [country]’ is where it was bottled. Look for ‘product of’ instead.

entries.title: Reading a nut butter jar
entries.question: What should be in a jar of peanut butter?
entries.decision: Nut butter that separates is just nuts; no-stir has added oil.
entries.why: No-stir texture comes from added palm or hydrogenated oil, and usually sugar with it.
entries.short_answer: Peanuts, and salt if you want it. That is the whole list on the good jars. No-stir versions get their texture from added palm or hydrogenated oil. Most also add sugar. Oil on top is the good sign.
entries.detail: The separation people complain about is what natural peanut butter does, because ground peanuts are peanuts and oil. Stabilizers fix the texture and turn it into a product with a longer ingredient list. Sugar shows up in most conventional jars, and reduced-fat versions typically replace the removed fat with sugar and starch, which is the opposite of the trade most people think they are making. The same reading applies to almond, cashew and sunflower butters. One or two ingredients on the back is the standard, and it is easy to find. Oil sitting on top is not a fault, it is the sign that nothing was added to stop it. Stir it in once, then keep the jar upside down in the fridge.
sources: FDA standards of identity for peanut butter, 21 CFR 164.150

MaraNatha “Nut Butter FAQs” https://www.maranathafoods.com/health-facts/nut-butter-faqs/ (a maker’s own label-reading page: oil separation occurs naturally when no ingredient is added to keep the oil from separating, so those jars need stirring; a small amount of palm oil is what keeps a no-stir jar together; without stabilizers a jar left warm for an extended period can become rancid, so refrigerate)
entries.kristy_take: Peanuts, and maybe salt. Oil on top means nothing was added to stop it, which is the point.
watch_out: A short ingredient list separates naturally and needs a stir before use. Palm oil or another added fat keeps a nut butter from separating on the shelf. That is what the ingredient line shows when it appears.
With no stabilizer in it, a natural jar left warm for a long stretch goes rancid. The fridge is where an opened jar belongs.
buying_tips: The list should read peanuts, and salt if you want it. Nothing else is needed.
Oil separated on top is the good sign. Nothing was added to hold it in.
No-stir means palm oil or hydrogenated oil was added. Check for sugar too.
Reduced-fat versions usually replace the fat with sugar and starch.
Store natural jars upside down in the fridge. The oil redistributes on its own.
Same reading for almond, cashew and sunflower butters.

labels_decoded.meaning: On a nut butter, generally the short-list version. Still read the back.
Palm oil or hydrogenated oil added to hold the fat in suspension.
Fat removed and usually replaced with sugar and starch.

entries.tier_note: What holds no-stir texture together is on the list. Wanting only peanuts is the standard.

entries.title: Grains beyond rice
entries.question: What else should I be buying besides rice?
entries.decision: Grains other than rice cook like pasta, in plenty of salted water.
entries.why: Bulgur, quinoa and buckwheat are fast. Farro and barley are made for soups and bowls.
entries.short_answer: Rotating grains is the cheapest upgrade in the pantry. Quinoa cooks in fifteen minutes and holds together cold. Farro and barley are chewy, made for soups and bowls. Bulgur takes ten minutes with boiling water and a lid.
entries.detail: Variety is worth it on its own terms, since different grains bring different textures and cooking times, and rotating them means no single crop is the base of every meal. That matters practically as well, because rice takes up more inorganic arsenic from soil and water than other grains, so it is the one not to build every dinner on. Most of these cook like pasta, in plenty of salted water and drained when tender, which is far more forgiving than the exact ratios rice wants. Buy them from the bulk bins where you can. Buckwheat is not wheat at all and cooks fast. Millet and sorghum are cheap and carry no gluten. Bulgur is the fastest of the lot. The bitter coating on quinoa’s hull is called saponin.
sources: FDA guidance on inorganic arsenic in rice

Jerry James Stone “Why You Should Always Rinse Quinoa Before Cooking” https://www.jerryjamesstone.com/2019/06/17/why-you-should-always-rinse-quinoa-before-cooking/ (quinoa’s outer hull is coated with saponin, a bitter natural coating, and rinsing before cooking is how it comes off)
entries.kristy_take: Cook them like pasta: lots of salted water, drain when tender. Far easier than getting a rice ratio right.
watch_out: Quinoa carries a bitter natural coating on its outer hull. Rinse it before cooking. That is what takes the bitterness off.
buying_tips: Quick ones: bulgur takes 10 minutes, quinoa and buckwheat 15, millet 20.
Chewy and slow: farro, barley, wheat berries, sorghum. Made for soups and bowls.
Buckwheat, millet, sorghum and quinoa carry no gluten. Barley, farro and bulgur do.
Cook most of them like pasta, in salted water, and drain.
Cook a big batch. They keep several days and reheat straight from cold.

labels_decoded.meaning: Some bran removed. Cooks faster, less of the whole kernel.
Bran intact. A longer cook, and it holds its chew.

entries.tier_note: Cook times and texture are properties of the grain, not a claim made about it.

entries.title: Buying bottled water
entries.question: Which bottled water should I buy?
entries.decision: Spring water comes from one named place; purified is treated tap.
entries.why: Spring water comes from a place. Purified is a process run on whatever came out of the tap.
entries.short_answer: Two products share one shelf. Spring water is defined by its underground source. Purified water is defined by its treatment, often of city water. Its label need not name the source.
entries.detail: The type on the label is a federal standard of identity, so it is the one word on the bottle that has to be earned. Spring, artesian and mineral name a source. Purified, distilled, deionized and reverse osmosis name a process. Mineral water is spring water carrying at least 250 parts per million of total dissolved solids picked up from the ground, and no minerals may be added to it, which is why the term still means something. Do not shop this on mineral content. Reverse osmosis removes dissolved solids by design, so a purified bottle reads lower on paper and that is the equipment working exactly as intended, not evidence against it. Provenance is the argument, and it is the only one that holds. Spring water is defined by where it came from: an underground formation that flows to the surface on its own, collected there or from a bore hole in the same formation, and carrying the composition that water had before treatment. Purified water is defined by what was done to it, which is distillation, deionization or reverse osmosis, run on whatever the feed water happened to be. That feed water is frequently a municipal system, and here the labeling rule does the arguing: a bottler drawing from a community water system has to say so on the label, unless the water was purified, which lifts the requirement.
sources: 21 CFR 165.110 — FDA standards of identity for bottled water: spring, artesian, mineral, purified, and the community-water-system labeling requirement

ANSES “Plastic particles in bottled drinks are caused by caps” https://www.anses.fr/en/content/plastic-particles-bottled-drinks-are-caused-caps (water averaged 4.5 particles per liter in glass bottles and 1.6 in plastic bottles and cartons; particles matched the paint on the caps; 287 particles per liter with uncleaned caps fell to 106 when caps were blown clean and 87 when blowing was followed by rinsing)
entries.kristy_take: Spring, in glass, from a place that can be found on a map. Everything else is a process wearing a mountain on the label.
buying_tips: A spring with a name and a town behind it. “Bottled at the source” means something when the source is printed.
Glass where the water is sold in glass. It is inert, it adds nothing, and it takes nothing.
“Mineral water” is spring water with the dissolved solids to prove the ground it came from. Nothing may be added to it.
Sparkling from a named spring is the same decision with bubbles in it. Read the label the same way.
“Purified”, “distilled”, “deionized” and “reverse osmosis” are processes. The source is not on that label, and it does not have to be.
watch_out: Not buying bottled at all is a defensible answer. A carbon filter on the tap is the same industrial treatment moved into the kitchen. It is the honest fallback, not the standard.

The cap is the contamination point, not the bottle. French food-safety researchers traced the plastic in glass-bottled drinks to the paint on painted metal caps. The caps were scratched by rubbing together in storage, before they were ever used. Cleaning the caps first took most of it back out. For water specifically the counts were low in every container, glass or plastic, glass slightly higher than plastic.
“BPA-free” on a single-use bottle is true and empty. PET was never made with BPA, so the words describe something that was never in the bottle.

labels_decoded.meaning: From an underground formation that flows to the surface on its own. Collected at the spring or from a bore hole in the same formation.
A treatment, not a place. It says what was done to the water and nothing about where it started.
Spring water carrying at least 250 ppm total dissolved solids from the ground. Adding minerals is not permitted.
Municipal tap. Required on the label, unless the bottler purified it, which removes the requirement.
True of every PET bottle and always was. PET is not made with BPA. The claim describes a plastic the bottle never contained.

entries.tier_note: The label definitions behind this are federal. The standard being held is about the source and the container, never a claim about health.

entries.title: Front vs. back
aliases: how to read a food label
entries.question: Where on a package should I actually be looking?
entries.decision: The front of a package is advertising; the back is regulated.
entries.why: The front is written by marketing. The back is written by law.
entries.short_answer: The front is advertising. The back is regulated. Front words like natural, wholesome and farm fresh come from marketing, and only some are legally defined. The ingredient list and Nutrition Facts panel have to be true. Turn it over first.
entries.detail: This is the one habit that makes every other label question easy. Nearly all of the confusion in a grocery store comes from front-of-pack language, which is written to imply more than it commits to, and almost none of it comes from the panel on the back, which is defined down to the font. Three things on the back do most of the work: the ingredient list in descending order by weight, the added-sugars line, and the serving size the numbers are based on. When the front and the back disagree, the back is the one that had to be checked. Every phrase on the front (natural, wholesome, farm fresh, made with real, lightly sweetened) is chosen by a marketing team, and only some of them have any legal definition at all. The ingredient list and the Nutrition Facts panel have to be true and have to follow a format. Turn it over first, and the front becomes noise.
sources: FDA food labeling regulations, 21 CFR Part 101
FTC guidance on food advertising claims
entries.kristy_take: The front is written by marketing. The back is written by law. Turn it over.
buying_tips: Turn it over first. Decide from the back, then look at the front if at all.
Ingredient list, added-sugars line, serving size. Those three answer most questions.
Front-of-pack words like natural, wholesome and farm fresh carry little or no definition.
When the front and the back disagree, the back is the one that was checked.
A short list of recognizable foods beats any claim printed on the front.

Regulated in content and format. The part that had to be true.

watch_out: Natural, wholesome and farm fresh carry little or no definition.
When the front and the back disagree, the front is the one nobody had to check.

entries.title: Ingredients are in weight order
entries.question: How do I read an ingredient list properly?
entries.decision: Ingredients run heaviest first, so the first three are most of it.
entries.why: The list runs in weight order. Split sugars keep any one of them from climbing it.
entries.short_answer: Ingredients run heaviest first, so the first three are most of the package. Everything after ‘contains 2% or less of’ is a trace, in any order. Watch for split sugars, each listed separately so none climbs the list.
entries.detail: The weight-order rule is the most useful thing on any package, because it turns a list into a ranking. A bread whose first ingredient is ‘whole wheat flour’ is a different food from one whose first ingredient is ‘enriched wheat flour’, whatever the bag says. The 2%-or-less clause exists because ordering trace additives serves nobody, and it also means everything below that line is a rounding error. Sugar splitting is legal and common, and the added-sugars line on the Nutrition Facts panel is the counter to it, because it totals them all whatever they were called. A product can list cane syrup, dextrose, juice concentrate and honey separately so no single one climbs the list, when together they would sit near the top.
sources: FDA Nutrition Facts label final rule (added sugars declaration)
entries.kristy_take: First three ingredients, then the added-sugar line. That is a whole label read in ten seconds.
buying_tips: Read the first three. They are most of the package by weight.
Everything after ‘contains 2% or less of’ is a trace amount, in any order.
Watch for split sugars: syrups, concentrates, dextrose and honey listed separately.
The added-sugars line totals them all, whatever each one was named.
A first ingredient of ‘enriched wheat flour’ is not ‘whole wheat flour’.

labels_decoded.meaning: The required order of the main ingredient list.
Everything after this point is a trace amount, and not in weight order.

watch_out: Everything after “contains 2% or less of” is a trace, and not in weight order.
Sugars get split across syrups, concentrates and dextrose so no single one ranks high.
“Enriched wheat flour” as a first ingredient is not “whole wheat flour”.
entries.tier_note: Weight order is required by law, which is what makes position readable at all.

entries.title: Judging any seal on any package
entries.question: How do I know if a seal on a package means anything?
entries.decision: A real seal names an outside auditor you can look up.
entries.why: A badge a company gave itself has neither. Each real seal covers one scope.
entries.short_answer: Ask three questions of any seal. Who set the standard? Is it published? Does an independent body audit against it? A company’s own badge answers none of them. No seal covers what it never set out to measure.
entries.detail: The gap between a certification and a marketing badge is entirely in the audit. Real programs publish their standard, so anyone can read exactly what was checked, and they send inspectors. The second half of reading a seal is scope: an organic seal covers inputs and practices and says nothing about welfare beyond a baseline, a welfare seal says nothing about pesticides, and a non-GMO seal addresses one issue only. Stacking seals on a package does not make it a better food, it makes it a food that paid for several audits. The ingredient panel still decides what the thing actually is. A badge a company created for its own products answers none of the three questions. USDA Organic, Certified Humane, Animal Welfare Approved, Global Animal Partnership, American Grassfed and the Non-GMO Project all publish standards and use outside auditors. What no seal tells you is anything it never set out to measure.
sources: USDA National Organic Program certification requirements
Certified Humane, Animal Welfare Approved and Global Animal Partnership published standards
entries.kristy_take: A badge a company gave itself is a sticker. The real ones publish, and they inspect.
buying_tips: Look for a named program, not a decorative badge. If the standard cannot be looked up, it is marketing.
Each seal covers one scope. Organic is not welfare, welfare is not pesticides, non-GMO is neither.
Third-party audited beats self-declared, every time.

entries.title: ‘Cold-pressed’, ‘expeller-pressed’, ‘refined’
entries.question: What do ‘cold-pressed’ and ‘expeller-pressed’ mean on an oil?
entries.decision: Cold-pressed oil is squeezed; refined oil is pulled out with solvent.
entries.why: Expeller and cold-pressed are both mechanical. Most supermarket oil is neither.
entries.short_answer: Expeller-pressed means a mechanical screw press with no solvent, though friction still generates heat. Cold-pressed is the same press with the temperature held down. Most supermarket cooking oil is neither. It is solvent-extracted, then refined, bleached and deodorized.
entries.detail: Extraction and refining are two separate steps and both matter. Mechanical pressing leaves more of the original flavor, color and aroma in the oil, which is exactly why unrefined oils taste like the thing they came from and refined ones taste like nothing. Solvent extraction pulls far more oil out of the same seed, which is why it dominates at commercial scale and why those oils are cheap. In the US ‘cold-pressed’ has no federal definition for most oils, so it carries less weight on a sunflower bottle than on an olive one. But the press only sorts oils that already clear the bar. Which oil it is settles the purchase first, and the pressing decides between two good ones after that. Two of these words describe pressing and one describes what happens afterwards. For olive oil in the EU, cold-pressed is a defined temperature limit.

FDA labeling regulations (no federal definition of ‘cold-pressed’ for most oils)
Food-science references on solvent extraction and oil refining
entries.kristy_take: Pressed oil tastes like what it came from. Refined oil tastes like nothing, on purpose.
buying_tips: Which oil it is comes first. Olive, avocado and coconut are the ones worth pressing well; a cold-pressed canola is still canola.

entries.title: ‘Sugar-free’ and what replaced the sugar
entries.question: If it says sugar-free, what is doing the sweetening?
entries.decision: ‘Sugar-free’ means something replaced the sugar rather than nothing.
entries.why: ‘Sugar-free’ is a defined claim about what came out. The list names what went in.
entries.short_answer: Something else, named on the ingredient list. ‘Sugar-free’ is defined as under half a gram of sugar per serving. The sweetness comes from a sugar alcohol or a high-intensity sweetener. ‘Unsweetened’ generally means nothing sweet was added at all.
entries.detail: ‘Sugar-free’ answers a Nutrition Facts question and says nothing about what took sugar’s place, which is why the ingredient list matters more here than on almost any other claim. Sugar alcohols appear by name and are also totalled on the panel; high-intensity sweeteners appear in the list and are used in tiny amounts. ‘Unsweetened’ has no formal FDA definition and in practice means no sweetener of any kind, including the non-caloric ones, which makes it the cleaner word to look for on yogurt, plant milk and apple sauce. ‘Naturally sweetened’ has no definition at all and covers honey, maple syrup and juice concentrate. Under ‘sugar-free’, the sweetness comes from a sugar alcohol (erythritol, maltitol, xylitol) or a high-intensity sweetener (stevia, monk fruit, sucralose, aspartame). ‘Unsweetened’ is the plainer word, and the two are not interchangeable.

entries.title: Seafood labels: wild, farm-raised, origin
entries.question: What has to be on a seafood label?
entries.decision: Seafood labels must name species, method and country, and still get swapped.
entries.why: All three are required on unprocessed seafood. Origin can mean where it was processed.
entries.short_answer: Most unprocessed fish and shellfish at retail must show the species, wild-caught or farm-raised, and the country of origin. Federal country-of-origin labeling requires it. The catch: origin can mean where it was processed, not where it was caught.
entries.detail: Country-of-origin labeling covers unprocessed fish and shellfish and is genuinely useful, since it turns ‘farm-raised, product of ___‘ into a readable pair rather than a guess. Two limits are worth knowing. Cooked, breaded or otherwise processed seafood falls outside the rule. And species naming has a long history of substitution, where a cheaper fish is sold under a pricier name, which is a far bigger problem on a bare fillet than on a whole fish or a piece with the skin left on. Buying whole, buying skin-on, and buying from a counter that can answer the origin question are the practical defenses. Country-of-origin labeling is one of the few places a store must tell you where food came from.
