entries.title: Serving size and the numbers under it
entries.question: Why do the numbers on the panel look so low?
entries.decision: The panel’s numbers are scaled to a serving the maker chose.
entries.why: Every number is per serving. Half of what looks reasonable is a third of the package.
entries.short_answer: Because every number on the Nutrition Facts panel is per serving. The servings-per-container line says how many the package holds. ‘About 2.5 servings’ means multiplying everything by two and a half. Serving sizes reflect what people typically eat.
entries.detail: This is the easiest number on a package to misread, and it is not an accident that it sits at the top in small type. The reference amounts are fixed by the FDA per food category, so competing products in the same category are genuinely comparable, which is the useful thing about them. What they are not is a recommendation. The 2016 label rules made serving sizes more realistic, put added sugars on their own line, and required dual-column labelling on packages that could plausibly be finished in one sitting. Read from the top down: servings per container first, serving size second, then the numbers. Serving sizes are set by regulation to reflect what people typically eat, not what is good for anyone, and larger single-serve packages now have to show a per-package column too.

entries.title: “Artificial color” and what it need not name
entries.question: What does “artificial color” mean on an ingredient list?
entries.decision: “Artificial color” is a category, not a color. Titanium dioxide qualifies.
entries.why: Certified dyes must be named. The rest may be declared as a group.
entries.short_answer: Two rules, split on certification. A certified dye must be declared by name, so “Red 40” always appears as itself. A color exempt from certification may ride as “Artificial Color” or “Color Added.” Titanium dioxide is one of those.
entries.detail:
The split is written into 21 CFR 101.22(k). Paragraph (k)(1) covers color additives subject to certification and requires each to be declared by the name in its own regulation, dropping the “FD&C” prefix but keeping “Lake” where it applies. Paragraph (k)(2) covers color additives not subject to certification and permits the collective terms instead, offering “Colored with ______” as the alternative that names the substance. Titanium dioxide is listed at 21 CFR 73.575, which sets the one percent ceiling and states that batches are exempt from certification.

So the generic phrase is a signal rather than a blank. Where a panel reads “artificial color” with no number beside it, the color is one federal rules did not require to be named, and the panel alone cannot say which. The declaration is legal and complete. It is simply less specific than it looks, and knowing what the category holds is the whole skill.

A certified dye must be declared by its own name, so “Red 40” and “Blue 1” always appear as themselves. A color exempt from certification does not have to: federal labeling rules let it ride as “Artificial Color,” “Artificial Color Added” or “Color Added.” Titanium dioxide is the white pigment used for opacity in candy shells, frosting, chewing gum and creamy dressings, capped at one percent of the food by weight. A label may name it outright as “colored with titanium dioxide,” and nothing requires that. The EU withdrawal turned on an unresolved genotoxicity question, not a demonstrated harm. JECFA reviewed the same additive in 2023 and found dietary intake no hazard.
sources: FDA 21 CFR 101.22(k) (declaration of color additives on the ingredient list)
FDA 21 CFR 73.575 (titanium dioxide: one percent limit, exempt from certification)
FDA, Titanium Dioxide as a Color Additive in Foods (color additive petition under review)
EFSA (2021), safety assessment of the food additive titanium dioxide E 171
entries.kristy_take: Named colors had to name themselves. The collective phrase covers the ones that did not. So “artificial color” stands where an ingredient would be: legal, complete, and vaguer than it looks.
buying_tips: Certified dyes appear by name and number. “Red 40” is always “Red 40.”
“Artificial color” and “color added” cover the colors that need no name.
“Colored with titanium dioxide” is that additive named on purpose, not by rule.

entries.title: Raw kefir
entries.question: Is raw kefir worth buying?
entries.decision: Kefir is milk fermented with live grains, and worth buying plain.
entries.why: A live ferment from a named herd. The refrigerated case is the only place it exists.
entries.card_why: Kefir is what a dairy does with milk it wants to keep, and it has been doing it for centuries. The grains turn it tangy and thick and it holds for weeks where the milk holds for days. The rule is the milk’s rule: the farm is the product. Buy it from the herd you would drink from raw, as close to the culture date as the case allows.
entries.short_answer: Raw kefir is a live ferment and it has to be sold cold. Anything shelf-stable was heat-treated after culturing, which ends the thing you were buying it for.
entries.detail: Kefir carries a wider mix of cultures than yogurt and pours rather than spoons. Made from raw milk it is the same sourcing question as the milk: a named farm, a small herd, a cold chain. Plain is the only version worth buying. The flavored tubs carry the added sugar of a dessert and the ferment becomes the excuse.
entries.kristy_take: Same farm as the milk, or it is just a drink.
buying_tips: The same farm name as the milk. Kefir is only as good as what went into it.
A culture or bottling date on the bottle, not only a best-by.

Raw dairy is not for every household. The raw milk card names who, once.
Kefir may carry a trace of alcohol. The yeast in the grains makes it during the ferment, and a live bottle keeps it.
Commercial bottles taste different because of what was added. Flavoring, additives and sugar make the difference, so plain is the one where the ferment is what you taste.

entries.title: Raw aged cheese
entries.question: Is raw milk cheese worth buying?
entries.decision: Raw-milk cheese aged past sixty days is legal and already stocked.
entries.why: Sixty days of aging is the federal line. Past it, raw-milk cheese sells anywhere.
entries.card_why: Aged raw-milk cheese is the raw dairy nobody has to hunt for. US rules allow it at sixty days and up, so a decent cheese counter already keeps a case of it. Sixty days of aging is a technology of its own. It is the reason an aged raw cheddar tastes of the place it came from. A young commodity block tastes of very little. The organizing principle is the milk’s: ask who made it, from which herd, and how long it sat.
entries.short_answer: It is the raw dairy nobody has to go looking for. US law lets raw-milk cheese aged sixty days or more sell across state lines. It sits in ordinary cheese cases. Most traditional European cheeses are made this way.
entries.detail: The sixty-day rule is why raw cheese is legal at US retail where raw milk often is not. Aging concentrates the cheese and develops it, and a raw-milk cheese carries the character of one herd and one season in a way a standardized pasteurized curd is designed not to. A staffed counter can usually name the maker, the animal and the age, which is exactly the information the rind label is too small to hold. Raw-milk cheese sits in the case beside everything else: no farm visit, no herdshare, no state-by-state map. Most traditional European cheeses are made this way, which is why so many qualify.
entries.kristy_take: Ask the monger who made it. A good one has been waiting to tell you.
buying_tips: “Raw milk” or “lait cru” printed on the rind label, with an age beside it.

entries.title: Sprouts
entries.question: Are sprouts worth buying?
entries.decision: Sprouts grow in the warm damp that bacteria also like.
entries.why: A living food sold warm is the only real problem. Cold case or your own jar.
entries.card_why: Sprouts are about as alive as produce gets, a seed caught mid-decision, sold days old. That is the appeal, and it is also the whole handling question. The warm damp days that sprout a seed are the same days that sprout everything else. A grower who keeps them cold from the sprouting room to the case is doing the only thing that matters. Past that, a jar and a screen on your own counter costs almost nothing. It puts the sourcing question entirely in your hands.
entries.short_answer: Cold case, roots still white, no sour smell in the clamshell. Anything sitting at room temperature has been given the conditions it was grown in.
entries.detail: Sprouting has been a winter green in kitchens for a very long time, and a jar with a mesh lid on the counter still produces a crop in three or four days for the price of a scoop of seed. Broccoli, alfalfa, radish and mung are the usual four. Buying them instead is fine when the case is cold and the turnover is quick; the clamshell tells you plainly when it is not, because sprouts go slick and sour before they look wrong.
entries.kristy_take: Grow them yourself and the sourcing question answers itself.
buying_tips: The refrigerated case only. Room-temperature sprouts have been left in growing conditions.
Roots still white and threadlike, stems crisp rather than limp.

The seed itself can carry the pathogen. The warm damp that sprouts it also multiplies any bacteria already on the seed.

entries.title: Strawberries and pesticide residue
entries.question: Are strawberries worth buying organic?
entries.decision: Strawberries have no peel to remove, so residue stays on them.
entries.why: Residue sits on the surface, and a strawberry has no peel to take away.
entries.short_answer: Strawberries are the strongest case in produce for buying organic: thin-skinned, eaten whole, nothing to peel. In a May 2026 lab screen, a conventional box carried 12 residues. The organic box came back non-detect. One box, tested once.
entries.detail: Independent testing commissioned in May 2026 screened two boxes of Driscoll’s strawberries, one conventional and one organic, at an EPA-certified lab for more than 500 pesticides. The conventional box came back carrying 12 residues, eight of them fluorinated compounds the testers classed as PFAS. The organic box came back non-detect. One box tested once is not a measurement of a brand, and it is still the cleanest picture there is of the choice made at the case. The residues were reported at levels prohibited in the European Union, Taiwan, Chile, Korea and Russia. The testers did not report them as over US federal limits and did not compare them to US tolerances either way, so what the screen shows is a comparison against foreign standards rather than a domestic violation. Whether fluorinated pesticides count as PFAS is contested in its own right: the structural definition used by the OECD covers them, and the EPA says they do not meet its own regulatory definition. Separately, Driscoll’s faces proposed consumer class actions filed in federal court in California in mid-2026 alleging it did not disclose PFAS-linked pesticide residues on its conventional berries, and a former food safety compliance manager has sued in Ventura County Superior Court alleging he was pushed out after raising pesticide compliance concerns. Driscoll’s rejects both sets of allegations and calls the consumer claims without merit. Nothing in either case has been decided.

entries.title: Root vegetables: carrots, potatoes, beets
entries.question: How do I choose and store carrots, potatoes, sweet potatoes, and beets?
entries.decision: Buy firm roots. Skip anything soft, shriveled, or sprouting.
entries.why: Firm is the freshness signal every root shares. Each guide says to pass on the soft, shriveled, or sprouting ones.
entries.short_answer: Firm is the test at every root. Potatoes: no bruises, nicks or soft spots, never green. Carrots: well colored, no green shoulders, wilt, flab or cracks. Sweet potatoes: smooth, even shape, even peel color. Beets: round, slender tap root.
entries.detail: Potatoes keep up to a month in a cool, dark place with good ventilation, ideally 45 to 50°F. Throw away any that turn shriveled or green or grow many sprouts. Sweet potatoes want cool and dry, 55 to 59°F: colder brings chilling injury (fungal decay, internal browning, shriveling) and warmer speeds sprouting. Carrots go in a closed bag or container in the refrigerator for up to two weeks. Cut the tops off first, since attached tops wilt the root, and a wilted carrot revives in a soak of cold water. Beets: trim the leafy stem to an inch, leave the root end on, and refrigerate in a food-safe container for up to two weeks. Carrots also sit on EWG’s Clean Fifteen, a standard ranking residues from USDA data, among the items with the lowest pesticide residues.

entries.title: Broccoli, cauliflower, and cabbage
entries.question: How do I pick fresh broccoli, cauliflower, or cabbage?
entries.decision: Dark green, tight, and unbruised. Soft or slippery is spoilage.
entries.why: Enlarged, opened, or yellowish-green florets mean broccoli past fresh, and a soft or slippery head is already spoiling.
entries.short_answer: Broccoli: dark green florets, closed, not yellowish or wilted, on stems that are not thick and tough. Cauliflower: no bruises or damage. Cabbage: strip wilted or insect-damaged outer leaves. A soft or slippery head stays on the shelf.
entries.detail: Broccoli is the short keeper of the three: refrigerate it in a plastic bag with holes and use it within three days. Cabbage goes the other way, staying fresh for several weeks in a plastic bag or wrap in the refrigerator at 41°F or below; before using, cut out the core and rinse the leaves under cool running water. Cauliflower gets kept away from raw meat and meat juices. By EWG’s Clean Fifteen, a standard ranking residues from USDA data, cabbage and cauliflower are among the fifteen items with the lowest pesticide residues.

entries.title: Onions and garlic
entries.question: How do I pick onions and garlic that will keep?
entries.decision: Firm and dry with papery skins, and nothing sprouting or moldy.
entries.why: A well-cured bulb has a dry neck and dry outer skins. A soft, scented, or sprouting one is already on its way out.
entries.short_answer: Onions: firm for their size, little to no scent, a dry neck, no cuts, bruises or mold, no sprouting. Some loose skins are normal. Garlic: clean, white or true to the variety, well cured, cloves firm.
entries.detail: Whole dry onions live in a cool, dry, dark place with plenty of air movement: no plastic bags, no wrap, and not beside potatoes or anything else that releases moisture. Storage between 41 and 75°F favors sprouting, so the cooler the spot the better. Refrigeration is only for sweet or mild high-water varieties, on a low-humidity setting, and a cut onion goes in a sealed container for up to seven days. Garlic keeps one to two months at room temperature in low humidity before it softens, goes spongy, and shrivels from water loss; it sprouts fastest between 41 and 65°F, and its odor moves into other foods, so it gets stored on its own. By EWG’s Clean Fifteen, a standard ranking residues from USDA data, onions are among the items with the lowest pesticide residues.

entries.title: Leafy greens: lettuce, spinach, kale
entries.question: How do I choose and keep lettuce, spinach, and kale?
entries.decision: Crisp, even color, no wilt, yellowing, or decay.
entries.why: Spinach is highly perishable and kale wilts in the warm, so the crispness of the leaf is the freshness date.
entries.short_answer: Lettuce: crisp, green outside, pale at the heart. Romaine: neither very loose nor very hard. Spinach: uniformly green and fully crisp. Kale: firm, deep colored leaves on moist, hardy stems.
entries.detail: Cold is the whole storage story. Romaine keeps about 21 days near 32°F and noticeably less at 41°F, so the coldest shelf of the refrigerator is the right one. Spinach wants 32°F too and will not hold good quality past two weeks; at 41 to 50°F it wilts and yellows faster. Kale goes in a plastic bag with as much air pressed out as possible, unwashed, for about five days; water on the leaves speeds spoilage, so wash at the point of use. On EWG’s Dirty Dozen, a standard ranking residues from USDA data, spinach carries more pesticide residue by weight than any other type of produce, and kale is on the list as well. At the shelf, lettuce runs bright to dark green outside and yellow or light green at the heart, free of insects, decay, or damage. A very loose romaine head is immature; a very firm or hard one is overmature. Spinach should be fairly clean with no serious damage. Kale should show no browning, yellow, or small holes.

entries.title: Bell peppers
entries.question: How do I choose and keep bell peppers?
entries.decision: Firm and evenly colored, free of cracks, decay, or sunburn.
entries.why: Firmness is a quality index on the postharvest sheet. A shriveled pepper has lost water in storage.
entries.short_answer: Green peppers: judged on size, firmness, and color. Colored peppers: at least half colored, firm, and uniform in shape and size. Skip any with cracks, decay, sunburn, disease, insect damage, or bruises.
entries.detail: Peppers keep best around 45°F, three to five weeks, and shrivel from water loss when stored warmer. At 41°F they hold about two weeks before chilling injury begins to show as pitting, decay, softening, or a discolored seed cavity; red and other colored peppers are less sensitive to chilling than green ones. Keep peppers away from raw meat and meat juices. A dark, sunken spot at the blossom end is blossom end rot.

entries.title: Apples and pears
entries.question: How do I choose and keep apples and pears?
entries.decision: Unbruised and undamaged. One spoiled fruit rots its neighbors faster.
entries.why: Damaged fruit spoils in storage, and spoiled fruit makes the sound apples and pears beside it ripen and rot faster.
entries.short_answer: Apples: firm and crisp, not mealy, free of bruising, decay, cracks, and insect injury. Pears: sound shape and size, free of bruising, insect damage, and decay. A firm green Bartlett is not a fault.
entries.detail: Cold and dark is the storage rule: 30 to 32°F is best and up to 40°F still works, in a ventilated box or a plastic bag with holes, unwashed, since the moisture from washing hastens decay. Gala apples soften quickly, so cool them fast; McIntosh and Honeycrisp are prone to chilling injury and want 38°F. Refrigerated apples keep up to a month. Keep apples and pears away from raw meat and meat juices. On EWG’s Dirty Dozen, a standard ranking residues from USDA data, both apples and pears appear. On apples, look for cracks at the stem or blossom end. Bartletts are picked mature-green and ripened off the tree; a ripe one is sweet, aromatic, and juicy with a buttery texture.

entries.title: Citrus: oranges, lemons, limes
entries.question: How do I choose and keep oranges, lemons, and limes?
entries.decision: Firm and smooth, free of decay, drying, or shriveling.
entries.why: Firm fruit with a sound rind is the quality index on the UC Davis citrus sheets. Decay and shriveling are the defects.
entries.short_answer: Oranges: even color, firm, smooth, free of decay and bruising. A partly green orange can be fully mature. Lemons: even yellow, smooth, firm, no shriveling. Limes: firm and smooth, no dryness.
entries.detail: Oranges keep at room temperature for up to a week and in the refrigerator for up to three weeks. Lemons hold best around 54 to 57°F and limes around 50 to 55°F, warmer than a refrigerator. A lemon or lime that has turned yellow is the one to use first: lemons picked fully yellow and limes picked yellow must be marketed quickly, while the fruit picked dark green keeps longest. At the bin, oranges should show even, intense color, free of skin blemishes and discoloration. A partly green orange gets its color from degreening, which does not change the inside. Lemons should be free of decay, drying, and rind stains. Green limes are preferred in the US, but yellow limes carry more juice; pick limes free of bruises and oil spotting.

entries.title: Stone fruit: peaches, nectarines, plums, cherries
entries.question: How do I choose and keep peaches, nectarines, plums, and cherries?
entries.decision: Unbruised and undamaged, with the skin color fully turned.
entries.why: Michigan Fresh gives the same instruction for peaches, plums, and cherries: buy fruit that is not bruised or damaged.
entries.short_answer: Peaches and nectarines: ground color turned from green to yellow. Plums: skin color turned for the variety. Cherries: at least light red all over, with green fleshy stems.
entries.detail: The optimum storage for all of them is just above freezing, 30.5 to 32°F, and Michigan Fresh puts cherries in the refrigerator at or below 41°F. Plums held between 36 and 46°F, the killing range, are more susceptible to internal breakdown: mealiness, browning, and failure to ripen. Peaches, nectarines, and plums picked well mature ripen on their own without ethylene; ethylene does not speed cherry ripening. Keep stone fruit away from raw meat and meat juices. On EWG’s Dirty Dozen, a standard ranking residues from USDA data, both peaches and cherries appear. A peach or nectarine with a flesh firmness of 2 to 3 pounds-force counts as ready to eat, and the same holds for plums. Dark skin staining is inking, a cosmetic mark from abrasion that affects the skin only. Cherries should be at least light red across the whole surface, with no cracks, bird pecks, shriveling, or decay; green, fleshy stems go with freshness.

entries.title: Mushrooms
entries.question: How do you pick good mushrooms?
entries.decision: Dry, firm mushrooms with no dark spots.
entries.why: Moisture is what spoils mushrooms. A dry, firm cap that is closed or slightly open is the fresh one.
entries.short_answer: Choose mushrooms that feel dry and firm, with no dark spots. Closed caps taste milder. Open caps with gills showing taste stronger. Keep them cold in a paper bag.
entries.detail: Penn State Extension, quoting a selection guide, looks for caps closed around the stem or moderately open, with pink or light tan gills. The cap surface should be white, creamy or an even light brown. Portobello is a large, mature cremini. Shiitake has broad, umbrella-shaped caps and is best cooked. Store mushrooms unwashed in the refrigerator, in the original container or a paper bag. A plastic bag or airtight container collects moisture that spoils them. Use fresh mushrooms within a week for best quality. Only an expert can tell poisonous wild mushrooms from edible ones, and no amount of cooking or drying destroys the toxins.

entries.title: Duck and quail eggs
entries.question: What should a shopper know about duck and quail eggs?
entries.decision: Cook duck and quail eggs until white and yolk are solid.
entries.why: Salmonella incidents involving duck eggs arise from time to time. Thorough cooking is the safeguard for any egg.
entries.short_answer: Buy them clean, uncracked and cold. Ireland’s food safety authority advises cooking duck eggs until white and yolk are solid. Quail eggs are tiny, about 10 to 12 grams each.
entries.detail: The Food Safety Authority of Ireland advises eating duck eggs only when thoroughly cooked. Raw duck eggs stay out of raw or lightly cooked dishes such as homemade mayonnaise or tiramisu. A duck egg is larger and heavier than a hen’s egg, so it needs more cooking time. In one test kitchen weighing, duck yolks made up 42 percent of the egg’s weight, against 32 percent for chicken. US FDA consumer advice for eggs: check for clean, uncracked shells, refrigerate, and cook until yolk and white are firm. Quail eggs weigh about 10 to 12 grams. In a storage study, quail eggs held at room temperature lost internal quality sharply, and the authors recommend refrigerated storage.
entries.kristy_take: A duck or quail egg is still an egg. Buy it clean and cold, and cook it all the way through.
buying_tips: Open the carton and check that every shell is clean and uncracked.
Buy from a refrigerated case and keep them cold at home.

entries.title: Sprouted whole grain
entries.question: What does sprouted whole grain mean on a label?
entries.decision: Sprouted grain labeled sprouted whole grain; no regulated definition exists.
entries.why: No rule defines “sprouted” alone. Sprouted grain that keeps the whole kernel is labeled “sprouted whole grain”.
entries.short_answer: No regulated definition of “sprouted” exists. Look for “sprouted whole grain” on the bag or flour. Sprouted grain that keeps its bran, germ and endosperm counts as whole grain.
entries.detail: A definition from AACC International (AACCI) counts sprouted grain as whole grain when it keeps all its original bran, germ and endosperm. The sprout must not grow longer than the kernel. Such grain should be labeled “sprouted whole grain”. USDA’s meat and poultry inspection agency, FSIS, accepts that definition. The whole grain claimed on a package is its dry weight, after the sprouting water is subtracted. A refined grain cannot sprout, because the sprout comes from the germ. Sprouting has to be a controlled process.

entries.question: How do you choose dairy at the store?
entries.decision: Pick the dairy type first, then read what the carton promises.
entries.why: Each dairy type has its own card. The carton then shows added vitamins, pasture and filtering.
entries.short_answer: Start with the type: milk, yogurt, cheese, butter, cream or a plant drink. Then read the carton. Vitamins A and D are optional in milk, so the label tells. Organic dairy animals must graze pasture.
entries.detail: Under 21 CFR 131.110, adding vitamins A and D to milk is optional. If vitamin D is added, each quart holds 400 International Units (IU), a measure of vitamin amount. entries.title: Olives
entries.question: How do you pick olives?
entries.decision: Olives cured in brine, which ferments them slowly.
entries.why: Fresh olives are bitter, and curing removes it. Brine curing ferments the fruit slowly, with water and salt.
entries.short_answer: Olives off the tree are very bitter, so they are cured before eating. Brine-cured olives ferment slowly in water and salt. Lye-cured olives are a milder style. Opened olives keep about 2 weeks.
entries.detail: Olives picked off the tree hold a very bitter compound called oleuropein. Curing leaches it out. The common curing methods are water, brine, lye and dry salt, and each gives a different texture and flavor. Water-cured olives stay slightly bitter, because water removes less oleuropein. Brine curing is a fermentation that turns the fruit’s sugars into lactic and acetic acids. It uses only water and salt, but takes a long time. Lye curing works quickly, and rinsing leaves a neutral olive that takes on flavors from vinegar and herbs. Salt gives olives their flavor and serves as a preservative. Salt curing has roots in ancient antiquity. Commercial table olives follow three main methods: Greek, Spanish and Californian. Greek-style olives are picked near full ripeness, at the purple stage, and cured in brine. Spanish-style green olives are treated with lye, rinsed, then fermented. California-style black ripe olives are lye-cured and darkened with air, then colored black with an iron salt. One review’s table puts debittering at 6–12 months for Greek, 1–7 months for Spanish and 1 week for California. The California method gives the mildest flavor and the least bitterness. USDA grade standards cover canned ripe olives (U.S. Grade A, B and C). USDA defines green olives as “completely fermented and cured” fruit of the olive tree.
entries.kristy_take: Cured the slow way, in brine, olives keep a salty, acidic, fermented flavor. Salt curing has roots in antiquity.

entries.question: How do you pick baking soda and baking powder?
entries.decision: Baking soda needs an acid; double-acting powder carries its own.
entries.why: Soda reacts with an acid at once. Double-acting powder carries two acids, one wet and one hot.

entries.detail: Traditionally, Neapolitan dough is made only of flour, water, salt and yeast. The flour is 00 flour, a soft wheat flour of medium strength. The dough rises at least 8 hours, in two phases. Dough balls run 180 to 250 g. They are stretched by hand only, never pressed by machine or rolled with a pin. The finished pizza is no wider than 35 cm. Leftover dough balls are thrown out each evening. The pizza bakes on the floor of a wood oven at 430 to 485°C, for 60 to 90 seconds. The wood must give off no smoke or odor: oak, ash, beech and maple. Well baked means golden and unburnt, with a bread-scented rim and a soft center that folds without breaking. “Verace Pizza Napoletana” is a collective mark, a name its own association governs. It is not a DOP, the Italian protected name given only to first-stage foods such as cheese and oil. Ready pizzas and frozen dough balls are spreading today. On a US label, “pan style” means a pizza marketed in a pan with a thick crust. “Sicilian style” means a thick crust, usually 50 percent or more of the pizza.

entries.title: Frozen fries
entries.question: How do you pick frozen fries?
entries.decision: Frozen fries of potatoes, oil and salt, with little else listed.
entries.why: At home, a hash brown takes potatoes, oil, salt and pepper. The bag’s list shows what else is in it.
entries.short_answer: Read the ingredient list on the bag. At home, a hash brown takes potatoes, oil, salt and pepper. Home fries take starchy potatoes and salt. Compare bags by what they list beyond those.
entries.detail: The federal grade standard describes frozen french fries as mature white potatoes, washed, sorted and trimmed. They may be cut or left whole. They are deep-fried or blanched in fat or oil, then frozen. Blanching is a short cook in hot water or steam. In a plant, the strips are peeled, cut and blanched, then par-fried, meaning partly fried, and frozen. Blanching also leaches sugars from the strips. The fries are finish-fried from frozen to develop color and crispness. Why it works: frying is first a dehydration process, meaning it drives water out of the food. The drier the food going in, the better the crust. So cooks fry once, freeze, and fry again. As food cools, moisture moves from the center to the surface. The second fry boils it off. The first fry also leaves simpler pathways inside, so water escapes more easily the second time. An air fryer is a convection appliance, meaning it circulates hot air. It cooks faster than an oven and gives a crisp outside. French fries cook well in one.
entries.kristy_take: A short list of potatoes, oil and salt is the standard here. At home, starchy Russets fry crisp once rinsed of starch and dried. Home cooks freeze fries after the first fry, then do the second from frozen.

entries.title: Frozen
entries.question: How do you shop the frozen aisle?
entries.decision: Keep frozen at 0°F; then ask about pizza, meals or fries.
entries.why: Food held at 0°F or below keeps its color, flavor and texture better than warmer food.
entries.short_answer: Buy only food frozen solid, and pick it up just before checkout. At home, keep the freezer at 0°F or below. For a closer look, ask about frozen pizza, meals or fries.
entries.detail: Food stored at 0°F or lower keeps its color, flavor and texture. Food held at 15°F may feel hard, but it is less solidly frozen than at 0°F. Over the same time, the 0°F food holds color, flavor and texture better. Freezing keeps quality but cannot improve flavor or texture. Processors flash-freeze food, which means freezing it very fast. Sellers keep it at 0°F or below to hold quality. Fast freezing makes tiny ice crystals. Slow freezing makes large ones that rupture cells, so moisture leaks out on thawing. Freezer burn shows as grayish-brown leathery spots where air reached the food. It can also show as white, dried-out patches that turn tough and dry. Folded foil can develop pinholes that let freezer burn in. Store shrink-film on meat breathes, so overwrap it to stop freezer burn. Freezer times and dates on frozen food mark quality only. “Do not refreeze” on a package is the packer’s quality advice. Quality can drop, and the packer cannot know home thawing conditions. Vermont’s rule has frozen display cases hold air at 0°F or lower. Each case there has a thermometer. A load line marks the top of the cold air at each end of the case. Cases sit away from door drafts, fans, lights and heaters. Thaw in the fridge, in cold water or in the microwave. Cooking from frozen takes about one and a half times as long.
entries.kristy_take: Freezing holds most of the quality food had when it went in, and never adds any. After the pick, handling is the shopper’s job.
entries.cart_pick: Packages frozen solid, picked up last
